title: 3D Pythagoras & Trigonometry
bodyMd:
# 3D Pythagoras & Trigonometry

## 3D Pythagoras & Trigonometry

> **Spec point** — `4.8D`

## 3D Pythagoras & trigonometry

### How do I use Pythagoras' theorem in a 3D shape?

- You can often find **right-angled triangles** within 3D shapes

  - If two sides of the triangle are known, you can use **Pythagoras’ theorem**

![Example showing Pythagoras' theorem used to find the slant height of a cone given its radius and perpendicular height.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/6b20aacf85e9-62167-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-1.png)

### Is there a 3D version of the Pythagoras' theorem formula?

- There is a **3D version** of Pythagoras’ theorem: $d^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}$

  - $d$ is the distance between two points
  - $x,y$ and $z$ are the distances in the **three different perpendicular directions** between the two points

![Example showing Pythagoras' theorem to find the diagonal in a cuboid (3D formula).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/9dbc131a3d83-18564-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-2.png)

- However, all 3D situations can be broken into **two 2D problems**

  - Form two right-angle triangles

![Example showing Pythagoras' theorem to find the diagonal in a cuboid (splitting into two 2D triangles).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/26a7724e33fa-30742-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-3.png)

![3DPythagTrig Notes fig3 (3), downloadable IGCSE & GCSE Maths revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/48caa509dd03-7523-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-4.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> You are not given the 3D Pythagoras formula in the exam.
> 
> You can always split 3D problems into two 2D problems (which don't need this formula).

### How do I use SOHCAHTOA in 3D?

- Again, look for **right-angled triangles** to use with **SOHCAHTOA**

  - You may need combinations of triangles that lead to the missing **side** or **angle**

![Example showing SOHCAHTOA to find the angle between the base and the slant height of a cone , given its radius and perpendicular height.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/88e64f4fd686-36187-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-5.png)

### How do I find the angle between a line and a plane?

- To find the **angle **between a** line **and a **plane**:

  - first **identity the plane** in the question
  - then **draw **on the** line** in the question (if it is not already drawn on)
  - form a **right-angled triangle **between the line and plane
  
    - The** height** of the triangle must be** perpendicular to the plane**
  - then use** SOHCAHTOA**
- The angle between a line and a plane is sometimes **not obvious**

  - If unsure, put a different point on the same line and see if it helps
  
    - Try to create a right-angled triangle
  - Some people like to imagine the line as a fishing rod, from which they lower the hook (and fishing line) vertically down to the plane!
  
    - Others like to imagine they are sitting inside the 3D object, looking around it (like corners of a room)

![Diagram showing how to find the angle between a line and a plane.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/dd83e8613318-15252-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-6.png)

### How do I apply 3D Pythagoras and trigonometry to more complicated problems?

- Always split up a complicated problem into **2D right-angled triangles**

  - Some questions may require more than one 2D right-angled triangle
- Some 2D triangles on the diagram are still drawn in 3D

  - It helps to** redraw **these 2D triangles **flat on the page** (not at angles)
  - You can then spot any uses of Pythagoras' theorem and SOHCAHTOA

![Example showing SOHCAHTOA to find the angle between a line and the base of a triangular prism. (Image 1).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/d4f35c853e7e-59348-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-7.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> If you are stuck in the exam with a complicated 3D diagram, it is always better to just start finding any lengths and angles in the shape, as:
> 
> - these may end up being useful,
> - you may score more marks than if you had left the question blank.

> **Worked Example**
> A pencil is being put into a cuboid shaped box.
> 
> The box has dimensions 3 cm by 4 cm by 6 cm.
> 
> ![A cuboid ABCDEFGH. AB = 3 cm, AD = 4 cm, DG = 6 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/28e71cc70f91-9470-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-8.png)
> 
> (a) Find the length of the longest pencil that can fit inside the box.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *The longest possible pencil will fit between diagonally opposite vertices, e.g. AF*
> 
> > *Form a 2D right-angled triangle, such as triangle ABF*
> 
> ![Cuboid ABCDEFGH with a right-angled triangle ABF highlighted and another right-angled triangle BEF also highlighted.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/7c6709083c2e-36773-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-9.png)
> 
> **Method 1**
> 
> > *To find the length AF, there are a few different options*
> *One option is to find length BF (from triangle BEF) then AF (from triangle ABF)*
> *Draw triangle BEF flat and use Pythagoras' theorem to find BF*
> 
> ![Triangle BEF, BE = 6 cm, EF = 4 cm, BF = a cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/49cf3762105f-10636-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-10.png)
> 
> $a^{2}=4^{2}+6^{2}\,a^{2}=16+36\,a^{2}=52$
> 
> > *Draw triangle ABF flat and use Pythagoras' theorem to calculate AF *
> 
> ![Triangle ABF. AB = 3 cm, BF = a cm and AF = b cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/11522c51cf53-38350-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-11.png)
> 
> $\begin{aligned}b^{2} & = & 3^{2} + a^{2} \\ b^{2} & = & 9 + 52 \\ b^{2} & = & 61 \\ b & = & \sqrt{61} = 7 . 81024 . . .\end{aligned}$
> 
> **Final answer:** **The longest pencil that can fit inside the box is 7.81 cm (3 s.f.)**
> 
> **Method 2**
> 
> > *Apply the **3D version** of Pythagoras’ theorem: *$d^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}$
> 
> > *The distance in the **x** direction is 4 cm*
> *The distance in the **y** direction is 6 cm*
> *The distance in the **z** direction is 3 cm*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}d^{2} & = & 4^{2} + 6^{2} + 3^{2} \\ d & = & \sqrt{4^{2} + 6^{2} + 3^{2}} \\ d & = & \sqrt{61} = 7 . 81024 . . .\end{aligned}$
> 
> **Final answer:** **The longest pencil that can fit inside the box is 7.81 cm (3 s.f.)**
> 
> (b) Find the angle that the pencil would make with the plane BEFC.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *The plane BEFC is the horizontal top surface of the box*
> 
> > *To see the angle between AF and the plane, form a triangle with side AB (which is a height perpendicular to the plane)*
> *The angle needed is marked *$c$
> 
> ![Cuboid ABCDEFGH with a right-angled triangle ABF highlighted and another right-angled triangle BEF also highlighted.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/184ab2b031e2-56890-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-12.png)
> 
> > *Triangle ABF is the 2D triangle needed, but it is currently drawn in 3D*
> *Draw triangle ABF flat on the paper and write on the lengths from part (a)*
> 
> ![Triangle ABF with sides AB (opposite) = 3 cm, BF (adjacent) = √52 cm and AF (hypotenuse) = √61 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/d3a008e713dc-24816-3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry-13.png)
> 
> > *This is now ready for SOHCAHTOA*
> *We know all three sides so could use any trig ratio, for example  *$\mathrm{tan}θ=\frac{O}{A}$
> *Use this to find angle *$c$
> 
> $\begin{aligned}tan  c & = & \frac{3}{\sqrt{52}} \\ c & = & tan ^{- 1} \left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{52}}\right) \\ c & = & 22 . 58853 . . .\end{aligned}$
> 
> **Final answer:** **The angle between plane BEFC  and the pencil is 22.6º (1 d.p.)**

title: Algebraic Notation
bodyMd:
# Algebraic Notation

## Algebraic Notation

> **Spec point** — `1.3A`

## Algebraic notation

### What is algebra?

- **Algebra **is a topic in mathematics that uses **letters **to** **represent **general** (or **unknown**) **numbers**

  - *x*  and *y*  are two unknown numbers
  
    - More information is needed to find their values
- Letters are also called** variables**

### How do I write calculations in algebra?

- Writing mathematical ideas in letters is called using **algebraic notation**
- You can use + and – to mean **add** and **subtract**

  - *a* + *b*
  *c* + *d* – *e*
- However** no** symbol is used for **multiplication**

  - *ab  *(means* a* × *b*) 
  3*ab*  (means 3 × *a* × *b*)
- **Fractions **are used for **division**

  - $\frac{a}{b}$ (means *a* ÷ *b*)
- You can combine the ideas above

  - $ab+\frac{c}{3}$ (means *a*×*b* + *c*÷3)
  - The **order of operations** for** **numbers still works
  
    - work out *a*×*b*  and *c*÷*3 * before adding them together
- **Powers** (**indices**) and **roots** are the same as with numbers

  - *a*<sup>2 </sup> means *a* × *a*
  4*a*<sup>2</sup>  means 4 × *a*<sup>2</sup>
  
    - With the order of operations, *a*<sup>2</sup> happens before multiplying by 4
  - $\sqrt{a}$ means the square root of $a$
- **Brackets** work in the same way as they do with numbers

  - $3(a+b)$ means $3\times(a+b)$
  
    - Add the *a* and *b* first, then multiply the result by 3

> **Worked Example**
> Raheem is playing a game and starts with *q*  points.
> He then earns a further 6 points.
> 
> (a) Use algebra to write down the total number of points that Raheem has.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Final answer:** **Raheem has ****q**** + 6 points**
> 
> The game then decides to doubles his total number of points.
> 
> (b) Use algebra to write down the number of points that Raheem now has.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Final answer:** **Raheem has 2(****q**** + 6) points**
> 
> > *You can also write:*
> 
> **Final answer:** **Raheem has (2****q**** + 12) points**

title: Algebraic Vocabulary
bodyMd:
# Algebraic Vocabulary

## Algebraic Vocabulary

> **Spec point** — `2.1A`

## Algebraic vocabulary

### What is a term?

- A **term** is either:

  - a letter (**variable**) on its own, or a variable raised to a power
  
    - For example, *x  *or* x*<sup>2</sup>
  - a number on its own
  
    - For example, 20
    - These are also called **constants **as they can't change value
  - or a number **multiplied** by a letter
  
    - For example, 5*x*
- The number in front of a letter is called a **coefficient**

  - The coefficient of *x*  in 6*x*  is 6
  - The coefficient of *y*  in -5*y*  is -5
- Terms can include **powers** and more than one letter,

  - 6*xy*
  - 4*x*<sup>2</sup>
  - *ab*<sup>3</sup>*c*

### What is a factor?

- A **factor** is any number or letter that **divides** a** **term** exactly**

  - There is no remainder
  
    - The factors of 3*x*  are 1, 3, *x*  and 3*x*
    - The factors of 4*xy*  are 1, 2, 4, *x*,  2*x*,  4*x*,  *y*,  2*y*,  4*y*,  *xy*,  2*xy*  and 4*xy*
- A term can be separated into **factors **that **multiply** together to give that term

  - Two factors of 5*x*  are 5 and *x*
  
    - 5 × *x* = 5*x*
- To **factorise **means to write something as a **multiplication** of **factors**
- When comparing two terms, a **common factor** is one that divides both

  - Compare 6*xy  *with 4*x*
  
    - Common factors are 1, 2, *x*  and 2*x*
    - The** highest** (or greatest) common factor is 2*x*

### What is an expression?

- An **expression **is an algebraic statement that does **not **have an **equals sign**

  - There is nothing to solve
- An expression is made by adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing **terms**

  - 2*x* + 5*y*
  - *b*<sup>2</sup> – 2*cd*
  - $\frac{6y}{5t}$
  - A single term is still an expression
- Expressions can be **simplified** (made easier)

  - *x* + *x* + *x*   simplifies to 3*x*

### What is an equation?

- An **equation** is an algebraic statement with an **equals sign** between a **left-hand side** and a **right-hand side**

  - Both sides are **equal** in value
  - For example, if 2*x*  has the same value as 10, then 2*x* = 10
- An equation can be **solved** by finding the values of the letters that make both sides equal

  - The equation 2*x* = 10 is solved when *x* has the value of 5
  
    - *x* = 5 is called the** solution**

### What is a formula?

- A** formula** is a rule, definition or relationship between different quantities, written in shorthand using **letters**

  - For example, weight, *w*,  is mass, *m*,  multiplied by gravitational acceleration, *g*
  
    - The formula is *w* = *mg*
- It is common to** substitute** numbers into a formula

  - But a formula on its own cannot be solved
- To turn a **formula** into an **equation**, more information is needed

  - For example, if *w* = 50 and *m* = 5, the formula *w* = *mg*  becomes the equation 50 = 5*g*

> **Exam Hint**
> - Knowing the differences between an **expression**, an **equation** and a **formula **will help you to understand the wording of exam questions.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) From the list below, write down
> 
> (i) an expression,
> 
> (ii) an equation.
> 
> 2*x* + 5 = 4              7*x *– 9            *x *= *vt* – *w*
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> (i)
> 
> > *An expression does not have an equals sign*
> 
> **Final answer:** **7****x**** – 9 is the expression**
> 
> (ii)
> 
> > *An equation has an equals sign and can be solved *
> 
> **Final answer:** **2****x**** + 5**** ****=**** ****4  is the equation**
> 
> (b) If *x *= 10, *v* = 2 and *w* = 3, use the formula shown to write an equation in *t*.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *x **= **vt** – **w**  is the formula shown (a group of different quantities forming a relationship)*
> 
> > *Substitute **x** = 10, **v** = 2 and **w** = 3 into the formula*
> 
> **Final answer:** **10 = 2****t**** – 3**

title: Collecting Like Terms
bodyMd:
# Collecting Like Terms

## Collecting Like Terms

> **Spec point** — `2.2B`

## Collecting like terms

### What happens if there is more than one term?

- **Terms** can be **added** and **subtracted **
- The** numbers **in front of the letters are called** coefficients**

  - If the coefficient is 1 or -1, then it is conventional not to write the 1
  
    - The coefficient of *x* is 1
    - The coefficient of -*y* s -1
- Each term has a positive or negative** sign** in front

  - In 2*x* - 3*y  *the coefficient of *x* is 2 (positive) and the coefficient of -3*y* is -3 (negative)
- **Subtractions** can be thought of as **adding** a **negative **

  - 2*x* - 3*y*  is the same as 2*x* + (-3*y*)
  
    - Just like 20 - 30 is the same as 20 + (-30)
- The **order** of two terms can be **swapped**, but the **signs** must** move** with their terms

  - 2*x* - 3*y*  is the same as -3*y* + 2*x*
  
    - A **plus** is now needed in front of the 2*x*
    - Just like 20 - 30 is the same as -30 + 20

### What is a like term?

- **Like terms **are terms with exactly the same** letters **and **powers**

  - The **coefficients** can be **different**
  
    - For example:
    - 2*x*  and 3*x*
    - 4*x*<sup>2</sup>  and 6*x*<sup>2</sup>
    - 5*xy  *and -7*xy*
  - These are **not** like terms:
  
    - 2*x*  and 3*y  *(different letters)
    - 4*x*<sup>2</sup>  and 6*x*<sup>4  </sup>(different powers)
    - 5*xy  *and 7*xyz  *(different letters)
- Remember **multiplication **can be done in **any order**

  - *xy  *and *yx * are **like** terms
  
    - So are 2*xy*  and 3*yx*

### How do I collect like terms?

- **Collecting like terms **means simplifying by **adding** or **subtracting **the **coefficients**

  - 2*x* + 3*x*  becomes 5*x*
  - 4*y* - 10*y * becomes -6*y*
  
    - A negative sign is needed here
- If there are **different** **types **of like terms, **collect** them **separately**

  - For 2*x* + 4*y* + 5*x* - 3*y*
  
    - Collecting the *x*'s gives 2*x* + 5*x* = 7*x*
    - Collecting the *y*'s gives 4*y* - 3*y* = *y*
    - The answer is 7x + y

> **Exam Hint**
> Don't leave terms like 1*x*  in your final answer in an exam - always simplify them to just *x.*

> **Worked Example**
> Simplify
> 
> $8a-5b-6a+4b$
> 
> **Answer: **
> 
> > *Collect the **a** terms first*
> 
> $8a-6a=2a$
> 
> > *Then collect the **b **terms*
> *Don't forget the minus sign in front of the 5**b*
> 
> $-5b+4b=-b$
> 
> > *Add together the two answers*
> 
> $2a+-b$
> 
> > *Simplify the signs*
> 
> $2a-b$

title: Substitution
bodyMd:
# Substitution

## Substitution

> **Spec point** — `2.2A`

## Substitution

### What is substitution?

- **Substitution** means **replacing** a letter (variable) in a formula with a given **number**

### How do I substitute numbers into a formula?

- Write down the **formula**
- **Replace** (substitute) the letters in the formula with the given numbers

  - If substituting in a **negative** **number**, it is important to put **brackets** around it
  
    - For example, (-3)
- **Simplify **any numerical calculations
- **Calculate** the final value
- Sometimes the result is an **equation **which you can then **solve**

> **Exam Hint**
> On your calculator, don't forget to put **brackets** around any substituted **negative** numbers!
> 
> Be careful with negatives and powers. For example, if $x=-4$ then $x^{2} = \left(- 4\right)^{2} = 16$.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Given that $x=2$ and $y=-4$, find the value of the expression:
> 
> (i)  $2 x \left(x + 3 y\right)$
> 
> (ii) $y^{2}+y^{3}$
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **(i)**
> 
> > *Substitute the numbers given*
> *Use brackets () around negative numbers*
> 
> $\begin{matrix} & 2 \times 2 \times \left(2 + 3 \times \left(- 4\right)\right)\end{matrix}$
> 
> > *Complete the calculation*
> *Show every step of working, following the order of operations correctly*
> 
> $\begin{aligned} & = & 2 \times 2 \times \left(2 - 12\right) \\ & = & 2 \times 2 \times \left(- 10\right) \text{   } \\ & = & 4 \times \left(- 10\right)\end{aligned}$
> 
> **-40**
> 
> **(ii)**
> 
> > *Substitute the numbers given*
> *Use brackets () around negative numbers*
> 
> $\left(- 4\right)^{2} + \left(- 4\right)^{3}$
> 
> > *Work out the powers remembering to include the brackets*
> 
> $16 + \left(- 64\right)$
> 
> > *Complete the calculation*
> 
> $16-64$
> 
> **Final answer:** **-48**
> 
> (b) The formula $P=2l+2w$ is used to find the perimeter, $P$, of a rectangle of length $l$ and width $w$.
> 
> Given that the rectangle has a perimeter of 20 cm and a width of 4 cm, find its length.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Substitute the values you are given for *$P$* and *$w$* into the formula*
> 
> $20=2\timesl+2\times4$
> 
> > *Simplify*
> 
> $20=2l+8$
> 
> > *Solve the resulting equation to find the value of *$l$
> *Start by subtracting 8 from both sides*
> 
> $12=2l$
> 
> > *Divide both sides by 2*
> 
> **Final answer:** $l=6\mathrm{cm}$** **

title: Adding & Subtracting Algebraic Fractions
bodyMd:
# Adding & Subtracting Algebraic Fractions

## Adding & Subtracting Algebraic Fractions

> **Spec point** — `2.2C`

## Adding & subtracting algebraic fractions

### How do I add (or subtract) two algebraic fractions?

- The **rules** for adding and subtracting **algebraic fractions** are the **same** as they are for **fractions with numbers**
- **STEP 1 **
Find the** lowest common denominator** (LCD)

  - Sometimes the LCD can be found by **multiplying** the denominators together
  
    - E.g. The LCD for the fractions $\frac{1}{x+2}$ and $\frac{1}{x+5}$ is $\left(x + 2\right) \left(x + 5\right)$
    - Similarly, with numbers, the LCD of $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{5}$ is 2 × 5 = 10
  - Although multiplying the denominators will always give you a multiple, it is **not necessarily the lowest** multiple
  
    - E.g. The LCD for the fractions $\frac{1}{x}$ and $\frac{1}{2x}$ is $2x$ (not $2x^{2}$) as both terms already include an $x$
    - Similarly, with numbers, the LCD of $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$ is just 4, not 2 × 4 = 8
  - Other examples include:
  
    - The LCD of $\frac{1}{x+2}$ and $\frac{1}{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 1\right)}$ is $\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 1\right)$
    - The LCD of $\frac{1}{x+1}$ and $\frac{1}{\left(x + 1\right)^{2}}$ is $\left(x + 1\right)^{2}$
    - The LCD of $\frac{1}{\left(x + 3\right) \left(x - 1\right)}$ and $\frac{1}{\left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)}$ is $\left(x + 3\right) \left(x - 1\right) \left(x + 4\right)$
- **STEP 2** Write each fraction over the** lowest common denominator** **Multiply the numerator** of each fraction by the **same amount** as the denominator

  - E.g. $\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{x - 4} + \frac{1}{x + 2} & = & \frac{x \left(x + 2\right)}{\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 2\right)} + \frac{\left(x - 4\right)}{\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 2\right)}\end{aligned}$
- **STEP 3** Write as a **single fraction** over the lowest common denominator and **simplify the numerator**

  - Do this by **adding** or **subtracting** the **numerators**
  - Take particular care if subtracting
  - E.g. $\begin{aligned} & & \frac{x \left(x + 2\right) + \left(x - 4\right)}{\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 2\right)}\end{aligned} = \frac{x^{2} + 2 x + x - 4}{\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 2\right)} = \frac{x^{2} + 3 x - 4}{\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 2\right)}$
- **STEP 4** **Check** at the end to see if the top **factorises** and the fraction can be** simplified**

  - E.g. $\frac{\left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)}{\left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 2\right)}$, the top factorises but there are no common factors so it is in its most simple form

> **Exam Hint**
> Leaving the top and bottom of your answer in **factorised form **will help you see if anything cancels at the end.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Express $\frac{x}{x+4}-\frac{3}{x-1}$ as a single fraction.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *The lowest common denominator is *$\left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)$
> *Write each fraction over this common denominator, remember to multiply the top of the fractions too*
> 
> $\frac{x \left(x - 1\right)}{\left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)} - \frac{3 \left(x + 4\right)}{\left(x - 1\right) \left(x + 4\right)}$
> 
> > *Combine the fractions, as they now have the same denominator*
> 
> $\frac{x \left(x - 1\right) - 3 \left(x + 4\right)}{\left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)}$
> 
> > *Simplify the numerator*
> *Be careful expanding with the negative signs*
> 
> $\frac{\left(x^{2} - x\right) - \left(3 x + 12\right)}{\left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)} = \frac{x^{2} - 4 x - 12}{\left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)}$
> 
> > *Factorise the top*
> 
> $\frac{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 6\right)}{\left(x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)}$
> 
> > *There are no terms which would cancel here, so this is the final answer*
> 
> $\frac{(x+2)(x-6)}{(x+4)(x-1)}$
> 
> (b) Express $\frac{x - 4}{2 \left(x - 3\right)} - \frac{x - 1}{2 x}$ as a single fraction.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *The lowest common denominator is *$2 x \left(x - 3\right)$* *
> *(You could also use *$4 x \left(x - 3\right)$* but this wouldn't be the **lowest** common denominator)*
> 
> > *Write each fraction over this common denominator, remember to multiply the top of the fractions too*
> 
> $\frac{x \left(x - 4\right)}{2 x \left(x - 3\right)} - \frac{\left(x - 1\right) \left(x - 3\right)}{2 x \left(x - 3\right)}$
> 
> > *Combine the fractions, as they now have the same denominator*
> 
> $\frac{x \left(x - 4\right) - \left(x - 1\right) \left(x - 3\right)}{2 x \left(x - 3\right)}$
> 
> > *Simplify the numerator*
> *Be careful expanding with negative signs*
> 
> $\frac{\left(x^{2} - 4 x\right) - \left(x^{2} - 4 x + 3\right)}{2 x \left(x - 3\right)} = \frac{x^{2} - 4 x - x^{2} + 4 x - 3}{2 x \left(x - 3\right)} = \frac{- 3}{2 x \left(x - 3\right)}$
> 
> > *There is nothing else that can be factorised on the numerator, so this is the final answer*
> 
> $\frac{-3}{2x(x-3)}$** or *** *$\frac{3}{2 x \left(3 - x\right)}$

title: Multiplying & Dividing Algebraic Fractions
bodyMd:
# Multiplying & Dividing Algebraic Fractions

## Multiplying & Dividing Algebraic Fractions

> **Spec point** — `2.2C`

## Multiplying & dividing algebraic fractions

### How do I multiply algebraic fractions?

- **STEP 1** **Simplify** both fractions first by** fully factorising**

  - E.g. $\frac{x}{3 x + 6} \times \frac{2 x + 4}{x + 7} = \frac{x}{3 \left(x + 2\right)} \times \frac{2 \left(x + 2\right)}{x + 7}$
- **STEP 2** **Cancel** any common factors on top and bottom (from either fraction)

  - E.g. $\frac{x}{3 \cancel{\left(x + 2\right)}} \times \frac{2 \cancel{\left(x + 2\right)}}{x + 7} = \frac{x}{3} \times \frac{2}{x + 7}$
- **STEP 3**
Multiply the **tops** together
Multiply the **bottoms** together

  - E.g. $\frac{2 x}{3 \left(x + 7\right)}$
- **STEP 4** **Check** for any further factorising and cancelling

  - E.g. $\frac{2 x}{3 \left(x + 7\right)}$ has no common factors so is in its simplest form

> **Worked Example**
> Write the following as a single fraction in its simplest form
> 
> $\frac{2x^{2}-11x+12}{x^{2}+3x-28}\times\frac{x^{2}-5x-14}{9-4x^{2}}$
> 
> **Answer**:
> 
> > *Factorise the four quadratics*
> 
> $2x^{2}-11x+12$
> 
> - *Two numbers that multiply to give 2×12=24 and add to give -11*
> - *-3 and -8*
> 
> 2 x squared minus 3 x minus 8 x plus 12
$>x\left(2 x - 3\right)-4\left(2 x - 3\right)$
$>\left(2 x - 3\right)\left(x - 4\right)$
> 
> $x^{2}+3x-28$
> 
> - *Two numbers that multiply to give -28 and add to give 3*
> - *7 and -4*
> 
> $\left(x + 7\right) \left(x - 4\right)$
> 
> $x^{2}-5x-14$
> 
> - *Two numbers that multiply to give -14 and add to give -5*
> - *2 and -7*
> 
> $\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 7\right)$
> 
> $9-4x^{2}$
> 
> - *Difference of two squares*
> - $3^{2} - \left(2 x\right)^{2}$
> 
> $\left(3 - 2 x\right) \left(3 + 2 x\right)$
> 
> > *Write the expression using the factors*
> 
> $\frac{\left(2 x - 3\right) \left(x - 4\right)}{\left(x + 7\right) \left(x - 4\right)} \times \frac{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 7\right)}{\left(3 - 2 x\right) \left(3 + 2 x\right)}$
> 
> > *Rewrite *$2x-3$* as *$- \left(3 - 2 x\right)$* and cancel common factors*
> 
> $\frac{- \cancel{( 3 - 2 x )} \cancel{( x - 4 )} }{( x + 7 ) \cancel{( x - 4 )} } \\times \frac{( x + 2 ) ( x - 7 )}{ \cancel{( 3 - 2 x )} ( 3 + 2 x )}$
$> \frac{ - 1}{ ( x + 7 ) } \times \frac{ ( x + 2 ) ( x - 7 ) }{ ( 3 + 2 x ) }$
> 
> > *Write as a single fraction*
> 
> - $\left(x + 7\right)$* and *$\left(x - 7\right)$* are not common factors*
> - *You can multiply *$\left(x - 7\right)$* by -1 to get rid of the negative sign in front of the front*
> - *Leave the expressions factorised*
> 
> $\frac{- \left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 7\right)}{\left(x + 7\right) \left(3 + 2 x\right)}  or  \frac{\left(x + 2\right) \left(7 - x\right)}{\left(x + 7\right) \left(3 + 2 x\right)}$

### How do I divide algebraic fractions?

- **Flip** (find the reciprocal of) the **second **fraction and replace ÷ with ×

  - So $\div\frac{a}{b}$ becomes $\times\frac{b}{a}$
  - E.g. $\frac{3x-12}{x}\div\frac{2x+8}{x+3}=\frac{3x-12}{x}\times\frac{x+3}{2x+8}$

- Then follow the same rules for **multiplying** two fractions

> **Worked Example**
> Divide $\frac{x+3}{x-4}$ by $\frac{2x+6}{x^{2}-16}$, giving your answer as a simplified fraction.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Division is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal (the fraction flipped)*
> 
> $\frac{x+3}{x-4}\div\frac{2x+6}{x^{2}-16}=\frac{x+3}{x-4}\times\frac{x^{2}-16}{2x+6}$
> 
> > *Factorise all numerators and denominators to see which factors cancel out*
> *You need to use the difference of two squares, *$x^{2} - 4^{2} = \left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 4\right)$
> 
> $\frac{x + 3}{x - 4} \times \frac{x^{2} - 16}{2 x + 6} = \frac{\cancel{x + 3}}{\cancel{x - 4}} \times \frac{\cancel{\left(x - 4\right)} \left(x + 4\right)}{2 \cancel{\left(x + 3\right)}}$
> 
> > *Multiply the remaining numerators and denominators together*
> 
> $\frac{1 \times \left(x + 4\right)}{1 \times 2} = \frac{x + 4}{2}$
> 
> > *Check to see if you missed any terms that are the same on the top and bottom that could be cancelled*
> 
> > $\frac{x+4}{2}$* is already in its simplest form *
> 
> $\frac{x+4}{2}$

title: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions
bodyMd:
# Simplifying Algebraic Fractions

## Simplifying Algebraic Fractions

> **Spec point** — `1.2A`

## Simplifying algebraic fractions

### What is an algebraic fraction?

- An **algebraic fraction** is a fraction with an** algebraic expression **on the top (numerator) and/or the bottom (denominator)

### How do you simplify an algebraic fraction?

- If possible, **factorise fully** the top and bottom

  - E.g. $\frac{2 x}{x^{2} + 3 x} = \frac{2 x}{x \left(x + 3\right)}$
- **Cancel** common factors

  - This factor may be a** single term**
  
    - E.g. $\frac{\cancel{x} \left(5 x - 1\right)}{4 \cancel{x}} = \frac{5 x - 1}{4}$
  - It could also be a **common bracket**
  
    - E.g. $\frac{x \cancel{\left(x + 2\right)}}{\cancel{\left(x + 2\right)} \left(x - 1\right)} = \frac{x}{x - 1}$
- A** common mistake** is to cancel a factor that is not common to **all terms** in either the top or the bottom of a fraction

  - E.g. The fraction $\frac{6x}{x+1}$ cannot be simplified
  
    - $x$ is not common to **all** terms in the bottom of the fraction
    - and the expression on the bottom cannot be factorised

> **Exam Hint**
> When asked to** simplify** an algebraic fraction, **factorise** top and bottom.
> 
> It is very likely that one of the factors will be the same on the top and the bottom.
> 
> Use this fact to help you if one of the expressions is difficult to factorise!

> **Worked Example**
> Simplify $\frac{4x+6}{2x^{2}-7x-15}$
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Factorise the top, by using 2 as a common factor*
> 
> $\frac{2 \left(2 x + 3\right)}{2 x^{2} - 7 x - 15}$
> 
> > *Factorise the bottom using your preferred method*
> *Using the fact that the top factorised to *$\left(2 x + 3\right)$* may help!*
> 
> $\frac{2 \left(2 x + 3\right)}{\left(2 x + 3\right) \left(x - 5\right)}$
> 
> > *The common factors on the top and bottom reduce to 1 (cancel out)*
> 
> $\frac{2 \cancel{\left(2 x + 3\right)}}{\cancel{\left(2 x + 3\right)} \left(x - 5\right)}$
> 
> $\frac{2}{(x-5)}$

title: Solving Equations with Algebraic Fractions
bodyMd:
# Solving Equations with Algebraic Fractions

## Solving Algebraic Fractions

> **Spec point** — `2.2C`

## Solving algebraic fractions

### How do I solve an equation that contains algebraic fractions?

- There are **two methods** for **solving equations** that contain algebraic fractions
- One method is to **add **or** subtract **the **algebraic fractions first** and then solve as usual

  - For example, to solve $\frac{8}{x+1}-\frac{5}{x+2}=1$
  - First subtract the fractions and simplify, $\frac{3 x + 11}{\left(x + 1\right) \left(x + 2\right)} = 1$
  - Then cross-multiply, expand and solve $\begin{aligned}3 x + 11 & = & 1 \left(x + 1\right) \left(x + 2\right) \\ 3 x + 11 & = & x^{2} + 3 x + 2 \\ 0 & = & x^{2} - 9 \\ 0 & = & \left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right) \\ x & = & 3  or  x = - 3\end{aligned}$
- Alternatively, you can **remove the fractions first** by multiplying everything **on both sides **of the equation by each expression in the denominators and then solve

  - For example, to solve the equation $\frac{4}{x-3}+\frac{5}{x+1}=5$
  - First multiply every term in the equation by both $\left(x - 3\right)$ and $\left(x + 1\right)$ and cancel common factors where possible
  
    - Multiply every term by $\left(x - 3\right)$ (this bracket goes in the **numerator **of any fractions)
    $\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{\cancel{\left(x - 3\right)}} \cancel{\left(x - 3\right)} + \frac{5 \left(x - 3\right) }{x + 1} & = & 5 \left(x - 3\right) \\ 4 + \frac{5 \left(x - 3\right) }{x + 1} & = & 5 \left(x - 3\right)\end{aligned}$
    - Then multiply every term by $\begin{aligned} & & \left(x + 1\right)\end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned}4 \left(x + 1\right) + \frac{5 \left(x - 3\right)}{\left(\cancel{x + 1}\right)} \cancel{\left(x + 1\right)} & = & 5 \left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 1\right) \\ 4 \left(x + 1\right) + 5 \left(x - 3\right) & = & 5 \left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 1\right)\end{aligned}$
  - Then solve $\begin{aligned}4 x + 4 + 5 x - 15 & = & 5 \left(x^{2} - 2 x - 3\right) \\ 9 x - 11 & = & 5 x^{2} - 10 x - 15 \\ 0 & = & 5 x^{2} - 19 x - 4 \\ 0 & = & \left(5 x + 1\right) \left(x - 4\right) \\ x & = & - \frac{1}{5}  or  x = 4\end{aligned}$

> **Exam Hint**
> When multiplying by an algebraic expression, use **brackets** around the expression, e.g. $\left(2 x + 3\right)$.
> 
> Multiplying by both denominators at once can speed up the process, but take care if choosing this technique in the exam!
> 
> Remember to multiply **every term** on either side of the equation.

> **Worked Example**
> $\frac{2}{p+3}-\frac{5}{p}=6p$
> 
> Show that this equation can be written as  $6p^{3}+18p^{2}+3p+15=0$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *To clear the fractions, we multiply both sides of the equation by each denominator *
> 
> > *Start by multiplying all terms in the equation by the denominator *$(p+3)$
> *The *$(p+3)$* on top and bottom will cancel in the first term*
> 
> $2-\frac{5(p+3)}{p}=6p(p+3)$
> 
> > *Now multiply all terms on both sides by the next denominator, *$p$
> *The *$p$* on top and bottom will cancel in the second term*
> 
> $2 \left(p\right) - 5 \left(p + 3\right) = 6 p \left(p + 3\right) \left(p\right)$
> 
> > *Expand brackets*
> *Be careful with negative signs*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 p - 5 \left(p + 3\right) & = & 6 p^{2} \left(p + 3\right) \\ 2 p - 5 p - 15 & = & 6 p^{3} + 18 p^{2}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Collect like terms*
> 
> $-3p-15=6p^{3}+18p^{2}$
> 
> > *Add *$3p$* and 15 to both sides of the equation*
> 
> $0=6p^{3}+18p^{2}+3p+15$
> 
> $6p^{3}+18p^{2}+3p+15=0$

title: Algebraic Roots & Indices
bodyMd:
# Algebraic Roots & Indices ## Algebraic Roots & Indices > **Spec point** — `1.4C` ## Algebraic roots & indices ### What are the laws of indices? - **Index laws **are** rules** you can use when doing **operations** with **powers** - They work with both **numbers **and **algebra** | **Law** | **Description** | **How it works** | |---|---|---| | $a^{1}=a$ | Anything to the power of 1 is itself | $x^{1}=x$ | | $a^{0}=1$ | Anything to the power of 0 is 1 | $b^{0}=1$ | | $a^{m}\timesa^{n}=a^{m+n}$ | To multiply indices with the same base, add their powers | $\begin{gathered}c^{3} \\times c^{2} \\ = ( c \\times c \\times c ) \\times ( c \\times c ) \\ = c^{5}\end{gathered}$ | | $a^{m}\diva^{n}=\frac{a^{m}}{a^{n}}=a^{m-n}$ | To divide indices with the same base, subtract their powers | $\begin{gathered}d^{5} \div d^{2} \\ = \frac{d \\times d \\times d \\times \cancel{d} \\times \cancel{d} }{ \cancel{d} \\times \cancel{d} } \\ = d^{3}\end{gathered}$ | | $\left(a^{m}\right)^{n} = a^{m n}$ | To raise indices to a new power, multiply their powers | $\begin{gathered}( e^{3} )^{2} \\ = ( e \\times e \\times e ) \\times ( e \\times e \\times e ) \\ = e^{6}\end{gathered}$ | | $\left(a b\right)^{n} = a^{n} b^{n}$ | To raise a product to a power, apply the power to both numbers, and multiply | $\begin{gathered}( f \\times g )^{2} \\ = f^{2} \\times g^{2} \\ = f^{2} g^{2}\end{gathered}$ | | $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{n} = \frac{a^{n}}{b^{n}}$ | To raise a fraction to a power, apply the power to both the numerator and denominator | $\left(\frac{h}{i}\right)^{2} = \frac{h^{2}}{i^{2}}$ | | $a^{-1}=\frac{1}{a}$

$a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^{n}}$ | A negative power is the reciprocal | $j^{-1}=\frac{1}{j}$

$k^{-3}=\frac{1}{k^{3}}$ | | $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{- n} = \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^{n} = \frac{b^{n}}{a^{n}}$ | A fraction to a negative power, is the reciprocal of the fraction, to the positive power | $\left(\frac{l}{m}\right)^{- 3} = \left(\frac{m}{l}\right)^{3} = \frac{m^{3}}{l^{3}}$ | | $a^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a}$ | The fractional power $\frac{1}{n}$ is the *n*th root ( `n-th root of blank`) | $n^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt[2]{n}$

$p^{\frac{1}{3}} = \sqrt[3]{p}$ | | $a^{- \frac{1}{n}} = \frac{1}{a^{\frac{1}{n}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt[n]{a}}$ | A negative, fractional power is one over a root | $q^{- \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt[2]{q}}$

$r^{- \frac{1}{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{r}}$ | | $\begin{gathered}a^{\frac{m}{n}} = a^{\frac{1}{n}} \\times m \\ = ( a^{\frac{1}{n}} )^{m} = ( \sqrt[n]{a} )^{m} \\ = ( a^{m} )^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a^{m} }\end{gathered}$ | The fractional power $\frac{m}{n}$ is the *n*th root all to the power *m,* $( \sqrt[n]{ } )^{m}$, or the *n*th root of the power *m,* $\sqrt[n]{( )^{m} }$ (both are the same) | $s^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left(s^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^{2} = \left(\sqrt[3]{s}\right)^{2}$

$s^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left(s^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = \sqrt[3]{s^{2}}$ | - These can be used to **simplify **expressions - Work out the **number** and **algebra** parts **separately** - $\left(3 x^{7}\right) \times \left(6 x^{4}\right) = \left(3 \times 6\right) \times \left(x^{7} \times x^{4}\right) = 18 x^{7 + 4} = 18 x^{11}$ - $\frac{6x^{7}}{3x^{4}}=\frac{6}{3}\times\frac{x^{7}}{x^{4}}=2x^{7-4}=2x^{3}$ - $\left(3 x^{7}\right)^{2} = \left(3\right)^{2} \times \left(x^{7}\right)^{2} = 9 x^{14}$ ### How do I find an unknown inside a power? - A term may have a **power involving an unknown** - E.g. $7^{4x}$ - If both sides of an equation have the **same base number**, then the powers must be equal - E.g. If $4^{3x}=4^{9}$ then $3x=9$ - And $x=3$ - You may have to do some **simplifying first **to reach this point - E.g. $3^{2x}\times3^{4}=3^{18}$ simplifies to $3^{2x+4}=3^{18}$ - Therefore $2x+4=18$ - And $x=7$ > **Worked Example** > (a) Simplify $\left(u^{5}\right)^{5}$ > > **Answer:** > > *Use *$\left(a^{m}\right)^{n} = a^{m n}$ > > $\left(u^{5}\right)^{5} = u^{5 \times 5}$ > > $u^{25}$ > > (b) If $q^{x}=\frac{q^{2}\timesq^{5}}{q^{10}}$ find $x$. > > **Answer:** > > > *Use *$a^{m}\timesa^{n}=a^{m+n}$* to simplify the numerator* > > $q^{2}\timesq^{5}=q^{2+5}=q^{7}$ > > > *Use *$\frac{a^{m}}{a^{n}}=a^{m-n}$* **to simplify the fraction* > > $\frac{q^{7}}{q^{10}}=q^{7-10}=q^{-3}$ > > > *Write out both sides of the equation* > > > $q^{x}=q^{-3}$* * > > > *Both sides are now over the same base of *$q$ > > > *So *$x$* must equal the power on the right-hand side* > > $x=-3$ > **Worked Example** > (a) Rewrite $\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{x^{4}}}$ in the form $x^{n}$ where $n$ is a negative fraction. > > **Answer:** > > > *Use *$a^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a}$* to rewrite the cube-root as a power of *$\frac{1}{3}$ > > $\frac{1}{\left(x^{4}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}}$ > > > *Use *$\left(a^{m}\right)^{n} = a^{m n}$* to simplify the denominator* > > $\frac{1}{x^{\frac{4}{3}}}$ > > > *Use *$a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^{n}}$* to rewrite as a term with a negative fraction as the power* > > $x^{-\frac{4}{3}}$ > > (b) Find the value of the constants $m$ and $a$ given that $\left(a x^{6}\right)^{\frac{1}{m}} = 8 x^{3}$. > > **Answer:** > > > *Use *$\left(a b\right)^{n} = a^{n} b^{n}$* to rewrite the left hand side* > *Remember to apply the power to both *$a$* and *$x^{6}$ > > $a^{\frac{1}{m}}\timesx^{\frac{6}{m}}=8x^{3}$ > > > *Both sides of the equation have a constant part, *$a^{\frac{1}{m}}$* and *$8$ > *And both sides of the equation have a part in terms of *$x$ > > > *The two sides of the equation are equal, so set the respective parts equal to one another* > > > *First,* > > $x^{\frac{6}{m}}=x^{3}$ > > > *The bases are the same, therefore the powers are equal* > > $\frac{6}{m}=3$ > > > *Solve to find *$m$ > > $m=2$ > > > *Then set the constant parts of both sides equal to one another* > > $a^{\frac{1}{m}}=8$ > > > *We now know that *$m=2$*, so substitute this in* > > $a^{\frac{1}{2}}=8$ > > > *Use *$a^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a}$* to rewrite as a square root* > > $\sqrt[2]{a} = 8$ > > > *Find *$a$* by squaring both sides* > > $a=64$

title: Completing the Square
bodyMd:
# Completing the Square

## Completing the Square

> **Spec point** — `2.7B`

## Completing the square

### How can I rewrite the first two terms of a quadratic expression as the difference of two squares?

- Look at the quadratic expression *x*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c *
- The first** two terms** can be written as the **difference of two squares** using the following rule

$x^{2}+bx$ is the same as $\left(x + p\right)^{2} - p^{2}$ where $p$ is **half** of $b$

- Check this is true by expanding the right-hand side

  - Is $x^{2}+2x$ the same as $\left(x + 1\right)^{2} - 1^{2}$?
  
    - Yes: (*x* + 1)(*x* + 1) - 1<sup>2</sup> = *x*<sup>2</sup> + 2*x* + 1 - 1 = *x*<sup>2</sup> + 2*x*
- This works for **negative** values of *b* too

  - $x^{2}-20x$ can be written as $\left(x - 10\right)^{2} - \left(- 10\right)^{2}$ which is $\left(x - 10\right)^{2} - 100$
  - A negative *b* does not change the sign at the end

### How do I complete the square?

- **Completing the square** is a way to rewrite a quadratic expression in a form containing a **squared bracket**
- To complete the square on *x*<sup>2</sup> + 10*x* + 9

  - Use the rule above to replace the first two terms, *x*<sup>2</sup> + 10*x, *with (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> - 5<sup>2</sup>
  - then add 9:  (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> - 5<sup>2 </sup>+ 9
  - **simplify** the **numbers**:  (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> - 25<sup> </sup>+ 9
  - answer: (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> - 16

### How do I complete the square when there is a coefficient in front of the x<sup>2</sup> term?

- You first need to take $a$ out as a **factor** of the *x*<sup>2</sup> and *x* terms only

  - **Factorise** the** first two terms**
  - $a x^{2} + b x + c = a \left[x^{2} + \frac{b}{a} x\right] + c$
  
    - Use **square-shaped** **brackets** here to avoid confusion with round brackets later
- Then complete the square on the bit **inside** the brackets: $x^{2}+\frac{b}{a}x$

  - This gives $a \left[\left(x + p\right)^{2} - p^{2}\right] + c$
  
    - where *p* is half of $\frac{b}{a}$
- Finally **multiply** this expression through by *a* (from outside the square brackets) and **add the c** on to the end

  - $a \left(x + p\right)^{2} - a p^{2} + c$
  
    - This looks far more complicated than it is in practice!
  - Usually you are asked to give your final answer in the form  $a \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$
  - For example,  *y *= 4*x*<sup>2</sup> + 16*x* + 5
  
    - Factorise out '*a*' on the right-hand side (use square brackets)
    
      - *y* = 4[*x*<sup>2</sup> + 4*x*] + 5
    - Replace *x*<sup>2</sup> + 4*x* with (*x* + 2)<sup>2</sup> - 2<sup>2</sup>  (because *p* = $\frac{4}{2}$ = 2)
    
      - *y* = 4[(*x* + 2)<sup>2</sup> - 2<sup>2</sup>] + 5
    - Simplify the terms inside the square brackets
    
      - *y* = 4[(*x* + 2)<sup>2</sup> - 4] + 5
    - Multiply everything inside the square brackets by 4
    
      - *y* = 4(*x* + 2)<sup>2</sup> - 16 + 5
    - Simplify to get the final answer
    
      - *y* = 4(*x* + 2)<sup>2</sup> - 11
- For quadratics like $-x^{2}+bx+c$, do the above but with *a* = -1

### How do I find the turning point by completing the square?

- Completing the square helps us find the **turning** **point** on a quadratic graph

  - If $y = \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$ then the turning point is at $\left(- p , q\right)$
  
    - Notice the negative sign in the *x*-coordinate
    - This links to transformations of graphs
    - A translation of $y=x^{2}$ by *p* to the left and *q *up
  - If $y = a \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$ then the turning point is still at $\left(- p , q\right)$
  
    - The *a* does **not change** the coordinates
    - The turning point is a minimum point if *a* > 0
    - or a maximum point if *a* < 0
- This can also help you **create the equation** of a quadratic when given the turning point

![Completing the square Notes Diagram 3, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/70ae26731145-8467-completing-the-square-notes-diagram-3.png)

- It can also be used to **prove** or **show** results using the fact that any **squared term**, such as the squared bracket (*x* ± *p*)<sup>2</sup>, will always be **greater than or equal to 0**

  - You cannot square a number and get a negative value
  - The smallest a squared term can be is 0

![Completing the square Notes Diagram 4, A Level & AS Level Pure Maths Revision Notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/96ce1435039b-25538-completing-the-square-notes-diagram-4.png)

> **Exam Hint**
> To know if you have completed the square correctly, expand your answer to check.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) By completing the square, find the coordinates of the turning point on the graph of $y=x^{2}+6x-11$.
> 
> > *Find half of +6 (call this **p**)*
> 
> $p=\frac{6}{2}=3$
> 
> > *Write **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* + 6**x** in the form (**x** + **p**)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **p*<sup>*2*</sup>
> 
> $x^{2}+6x$* is the same as *$\left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 3^{2}$
> 
> > *Put this result into the equation of the curve*
> 
> $y = \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 3^{2} - 11$
> 
> > *Simplify the numbers*
> 
> $y = \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 20$
> 
> > *Use the fact that the turning point of *$y = \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$* is at *$\left(- p , q\right)$* *
> *Here **p** = 3 and **q **= -20*
> 
> **Final answer:** **turning point at (-3, -20)**
> 
> (b)  Write $-3x^{2}+12x+24$ in the form $a \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$.
> 
> > *Factorise -3 out of the first two terms only*
> *Use square-shaped brackets*
> 
> $- 3 \left[x^{2} - 4 x\right] + 24$
> 
> > *Complete the square on the **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* - 4**x** inside the brackets*
> *Write in the form (**x** + **p**)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **p*<sup>*2*</sup>* where **p** is half of -4*
> 
> $- 3 \left[\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - \left(- 2\right)^{2}\right] + 24$
> 
> > *Simplify the numbers inside the brackets*
> *(-2)*<sup>*2*</sup>* is 4*
> 
> $- 3 \left[\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 4\right] + 24$
> 
> *Multiply -3 by all the terms inside the square brackets*
> (*You do not multiply -3 by the 24)*
> 
> $- 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 12 + 24$
> 
> > *Simplify the numbers*
> 
> $- 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 36$
> 
> > *This is now in the form **a**(**x** + **p**)*<sup>*2*</sup>* + **q** where **a **= -3, **p** = -2 and **q** = 36*
> 
> $-3(x-2)^{2}+36$

title: Expanding Double Brackets
bodyMd:
# Expanding Double Brackets

## Expanding Two Brackets

> **Spec point** — `2.2E`

## Expanding two brackets

### How do I expand two brackets?

- **Every term** in the** first** bracket must be multiplied by **every term** in the **second** bracket

  - Expanding (*x * + 1)(*x*  + 3) requires 4 multiplications in total
  
    - *x*(*x*  + 1) + 3(*x * + 1)
    - *x*×*x *+ 1*x* + 3*x* + 3
    - *x*<sup>2</sup>  + 4*x*  + 3

#### Using a grid

- You can use a **grid **for a visual way to expand brackets
- To expand (*x*  + 1)(*x*  + 3), write out the brackets as **row **and **column headings** of a grid |   | ***x*** | **+1** |
|---|---|---|
| ***x*** |   |   |
| **+3** |   |   |

  - They can be in either direction
  - Remember to write the appropriate **sign** in front of each term
- For each cell in the grid,** multiply** the term in the **row **heading by the term in the** column** heading |   | ***x*** | **+1** |
|---|---|---|
| ***x*** | *x*<sup>2</sup> | *x* |
| **+3** | 3*x* | 3 |
- **Add **together all the terms** inside** the grid to get the answer

  - *x*<sup>2</sup>  + *x*  + 3*x*  + 3
- Collect **like **terms
- *x*<sup>2</sup>  + 4*x*  + 3

#### Using FOIL

- **Every term** in the** first** bracket must be multiplied by **every term** in the **second** bracket

  - Expanding (*x * + 1)(*x*  + 3) requires 4 multiplications in total
- A good way to remember all the multiplications is **FOIL**

  - **F = First**: multiply together the **first** terms in each bracket
  - **O = Outside**: multiply the first term in the first bracket by the last term in the last bracket
  
    - Visually, these are the **outer** terms
  - **I = Inside**: multiply the last term in the first bracket by the first term in the last bracket
  
    - Visually, these are the **inner** terms
  - **L = Last**: multiply together the **last** terms in each bracket
- It helps to put **negative **terms in **brackets** when multiplying
- **Simplify** the final answer by **collecting like terms **(if there are any)

### How do I expand when there are multiple variables?

- All the same rules and methods apply as when there is just one variable
- Remember to only simplify **like terms**
- For example: $\left(3 x + 2 y\right) \left(4 x - 6 y\right)$

  - Expanding: $12x^{2}-18xy+8xy-12y^{2}$
  - The $xy$ terms can be combined
  - $12x^{2}-10xy-12y^{2}$

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Expand  $\left(2 x - 3\right) \left(x + 4\right)$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Using FOIL, multiply together the first, outer, inner and last terms*
> 
> $\begin{matrix}\textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } F \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } O \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } I \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } L \\ \boxed{2 x \times x} + \boxed{2 x \times 4} + \boxed{\left(- 3\right) \times x} + \boxed{\left(- 3\right) \times 4}\end{matrix}$
> 
> > *Simplify each term*
> 
> $2x^{2}+8x-3x-12$
> 
> > *Collect like terms (the 8**x** and -3**x**)*
> 
> $2x^{2}+5x-12$
> 
> (b) Expand  $\left(x - 3\right) \left(3 x - 5\right)$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Using FOIL, multiply together the first, outer, inner and last terms*
> 
> $\begin{matrix}\textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } F \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } O \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } I \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } L \\ \boxed{x \times 3 x} + \boxed{x \times \left(- 5\right)} + \boxed{\left(- 3\right) \times 3 x} + \boxed{\left(- 3\right) \times \left(- 5\right)}\end{matrix}$
> 
> > *Simplify each term*
> 
> $3x^{2}-5x-9x+15$
> 
> > *Collect like terms (the -5**x** and -9**x**)*
> 
> $3x^{2}-14x+15$

> **Worked Example**
> Expand $\left(3 r + 2 t\right) \left(5 t - 8 r\right)$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Expand using your chosen method, here we will use a grid*
> 
> |   | $3r$ | $+2t$ |
> |---|---|---|
> | $5t$ |   |   |
> | $-8r$ |   |   |
> 
> > *Work out the term in each place in the grid by multiplying*
> 
> |   | $3r$ | $+2t$ |
> |---|---|---|
> | $5t$ | $15rt$ | $10t^{2}$ |
> | $-8r$ | $-24r^{2}$ | $-16rt$ |
> 
> > *So the expanded expression is*
> 
> $10t^{2}+15rt-16rt-24r^{2}$
> 
> > *The *$rt$* terms can be combined*
> 
> $10t^{2}-rt-24r^{2}$

## Expanding Squared Brackets

> **Spec point** — `2.2E`

## Expanding squared brackets

### How do I expand a bracket squared?

- Remember that a **square** number is a number multiplied by itself
- Write (*x* + 3)<sup>2</sup> as (*x *+ 3)(*x* + 3) and use one of the methods above

  - With FOIL: (*x* + 3)(*x* + 3) = *x*<sup>2 </sup>+ 3*x* + 3*x* + 9
  - Then collect like terms: *x*<sup>2</sup> + 6*x* + 9

> **Exam Hint**
> Do not make the common mistake of saying $\left(x + y\right)^{2}$ is the same as $x^{2}+y^{2}$. In general, this is not true.

> **Worked Example**
> Expand  $\left(2 x + 3\right)^{2}$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Remember that the answer is not (2**x**)*<sup>*2*</sup>* + 3*<sup>*2*</sup>
> *Rewrite the expression as two separate brackets multiplied together*
> 
> $\left(2 x + 3\right) \left(2 x + 3\right)$
> 
> > *Using FOIL, multiply together the first, outer, inner and last terms*
> 
> $\begin{matrix}\textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } F \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } O \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } I \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } \textrm{ } L \\ \boxed{2 x \times 2 x} + \boxed{2 x \times 3} + \boxed{3 \times 2 x} + \boxed{3 \times 3}\end{matrix}$
> 
> > *Simplify each term*
> 
> $4x^{2}+6x+6x+9$
> 
> > *Collect like terms (the 6**x** and 6**x**)*
> 
> $4x^{2}+12x+9$

title: Expanding & Simplifying Single Brackets
bodyMd:
# Expanding & Simplifying Single Brackets

## Expanding One Bracket

> **Spec point** — `2.2C`

## Expanding one bracket

### How do I expand a bracket?

- The expression 3*x *(*x* + 2) means 3*x*  **multiplied by** the bracket (*x* + 2)

  - 3*x  *is the term **outside** the bracket
  
    - this is sometimes called a **factor**
  - and *x* + 2 are the terms **inside **the bracket
- Expanding the brackets means **multiplying** the **outside term **by** each term **on the **inside**

  - This will** remove** (get rid of) the **brackets**
  - 3*x *(*x* + 2) expands to $3x\timesx+3x\times2$ which simplifies to $3x^{2}+6x$
- Beware of **minus signs**

  - Remember the rules
  −  ×  −  =  +
  −  ×  +  =  −
  - It helps to put **brackets** around **negative** terms

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Expand  $4 x \left(2 x - 3\right)$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> *Multiply the *$4x$* term outside the brackets by both terms inside the brackets*
> 
> $4 x \times 2 x + 4 x \times \left(- 3\right)$
> 
> > *Simplify*
> 
> $8x^{2}-12x$
> 
> (b) Expand  $- 7 x \left(4 - 5 y\right)$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Multiply the *$-7x$* outside the brackets by both terms inside the brackets*
> 
> $\left(- 7 x\right) \times 4 + \left(- 7 x\right) \times \left(- 5 y\right)$
> 
> > *Simplify and remember that multiplying two negatives gives a positive*
> 
> $-28x+35xy$

## Expand & Simplify

> **Spec point** — `2.2B`

## Expand & simplify

### How do I simplify brackets that are added together?

- First **expand** both brackets **separately**

  - $4 \left(x + 7\right) + 5 x \left(3 - x\right)$
  
    - The **first** set of brackets expands to $4\timesx+4\times7$ which **simplifies** to $4x+28$
    - The **second **set of brackets expands to $5 x \times 3 + 5 x \times \left(- x\right)$ which **simplifies **to $15x-5x^{2}$
    - So $4 \left(x + 7\right) + 5 x \left(3 - x\right) = 4 x + 28 + 15 x - 5 x^{2}$
- Then **collect like terms**

  - $4x+15x=19x$
  
    - The other two terms are **not** like terms
  - So $4 \left(x + 7\right) + 5 x \left(3 - x\right) = 19 x + 28 - 5 x^{2}$

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Expand and simplify  $2 \left(x + 5\right) + 3 x \left(x - 8\right)$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Expand each set of brackets separately*
> 
> > *You can keep negative terms inside brackets*
> 
> $2 \times x + 2 \times 5 + 3 x \times x + 3 x \times \left(- 8\right)$
> 
> > *Simplify each term*
> 
> $2x+10+3x^{2}-24x$
> 
> > *Collect like terms (the 2**x** and the -24**x**)*
> 
> $-22x+10+3x^{2}$
> 
> (b) Expand and simplify  $3 x \left(x + 2\right) - 7 \left(x - 6\right)$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Expand each set of brackets separately*
> *Be careful: the second set of brackets has a -7 in front, not +7*
> 
> * *$3 x \times x + 3 x \times 2 + \left(- 7\right) \times x + \left(- 7\right) \times \left(- 6\right)$
> 
> > *Simplify each term*
> *Remember that multiplying two negatives gives a positive*
> 
> $3x^{2}+6x-7x+42$
> 
> > *Collect like terms*
> 
> $3x^{2}-x+42$

title: Expanding Triple Brackets
bodyMd:
# Expanding Triple Brackets

## Expanding Three Brackets

> **Spec point** — `2.2E`

## Expanding three brackets

### How do I expand three brackets?

- Multiply out any** two of the brackets **using a standard method and **simplify**
- Then multiply the resulting expression by the third (unused) bracket
- This step often looks like (*x* + *a*)(*x*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c*)
- Every term in the first bracket must be multiplied with every term in the second bracket
- A **grid **can help to keep track of all the terms

  - E.g. (*x* + 2)(*x*<sup>2</sup> + 3*x* + 1) |   | ***x***<sup>**2**</sup> | **+3*****x*** | **+1** |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | ***x*** | *x*<sup>3</sup> | 3*x*<sup>2</sup> | *x* |
  | **+2** | 2*x*<sup>2</sup> | 6*x* | 2 |

- Add all the terms inside the grid together

  - *x*<sup>3</sup> + 2*x*<sup>2 </sup>+ 3*x*<sup>2</sup> + 6*x *+ *x* + 2
- **Simplify **by collecting any like terms

  - *x*<sup>3</sup> + 5*x*<sup>2</sup> + 7*x* + 2

> **Worked Example**
> Expand  $\left(2 x - 3\right) \left(x + 4\right) \left(3 x - 1\right)$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Expand and simplify the first two brackets, for example using the FOIL method *
> 
> $\begin{aligned} & & \left(2 x - 3\right) \left(x + 4\right) \\ & = & 2 x \times x + 2 x \times 4 + \left(- 3\right) \times x + \left(- 3\right) \times 4 \\ & = & 2 x^{2} + 8 x - 3 x - 12 \\ & = & 2 x^{2} + 5 x - 12\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Rewrite the original expression with the first two brackets expanded*
> 
> $\left(2 x^{2} + 5 x - 12\right) \left(3 x - 1\right)$
> 
> > *Multiply all of the terms in the first set of brackets by all of the terms in the second set of brackets*
> 
> > *A grid can help when there are many terms to multiply together (e.g. write *$2x^{2}+5x-12$* in the vertical column and *$3x-1$* in the horizontal column, then multiply corresponding terms)*
> 
> |   | $3x$ | $-1$ |
> |---|---|---|
> | $2x^{2}$ | $6x^{3}$ | $-2x^{2}$ |
> | $5x$ | $15x^{2}$ | $-5x$ |
> | $-12$ | $-36x$ | $12$ |
> 
> > *Write out the multiplied terms*
> 
> $6x^{3}-2x^{2}+15x^{2}-5x-36x+12$
> 
> > *Collect the like terms to simplify*
> 
> $6x^{3}+13x^{2}-41x+12$

title: Deciding the Factorisation Method
bodyMd:
# Deciding the Factorisation Method

## Quadratics Factorising Methods

> **Spec point** — `2.2F`

## Quadratics factorising methods

### How do I know if an expression factorises?

- The easiest way to check if *ax*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c* factorises is to check if you can find a pair of integers which:

  - Multiply to give *ac*
  - Sum to give *b*
  - If you can find integers to satisfy this, the expression must factorise
- There are some alternate methods to check:

  - Method 1: Use a **calculator **to solve the quadratic expression equal to 0
  
    - Only some calculators have this functionality
    - If the **solutions are integers or fractions** (without square roots), then the quadratic expression will factorise
  - Method 2: Find the value under the square root in the quadratic formula
  
    - ***b***<sup>**2**</sup>** – 4*****ac***
    - If this number is a **square number**, then the quadratic expression will factorise

### Which factorisation method should I use for a quadratic expression?

- Does it have **2 terms only**?

  - Yes, like $x^{2}-7x$
  
    - Factorise out the highest common factor, *x*
    - $x \left(x - 7\right)$
  - Yes, like $x^{2}-9$
  
    - Use the "difference of two squares" to factorise
    - $\left(x + 3\right) \left(x - 3\right)$

Does it have **3 terms**?

- Yes, starting with *x*<sup>2</sup> like $x^{2}-3x-10$

  - Use "factorising simple quadratics" by finding two numbers that add to -3 and multiply to -10
  - $\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 5\right)$
- Yes, starting with *ax*<sup>2</sup> like $3x^{2}+15x+18$

  - Check to see if the 3 in front of *x*<sup>2</sup> is a** common factor **for** all three** **terms **(which it is in this case), then **factorise it out **of all three terms
  - $3 \left(x^{2} + 5 x + 6\right)$
  - The quadratic expression inside the brackets is now *x*<sup>2</sup> +... , which factorises more easily
  - $3 \left(x + 2\right) \left(x + 3\right)$
- Yes, starting with *ax*<sup>2</sup> like $3x^{2}-5x-2$

  - The 3 in front of *x*<sup>2</sup> is not a** **common factor for all three term
  - Use "factorising harder quadratics", for example factorising by grouping or factorising using a grid
  - $\left(3 x + 1\right) \left(x - 2\right)$

### What other expressions should I be able to factorise?

- You may have a** cubed term **like $x^{3}-3x^{2}-10x$

  - Check to see if *x* is a** common factor **for** all three** **terms **(which it is in this case), so **factorise it out **of all three terms
  - $x \left(x^{2} - 3 x - 10\right)$
  - The remaining quadratic can then be factorised
  - $x \left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 5\right)$
- It can also be useful to spot a quadratic in the form $x^{2}+2ax+a^{2}$

  - This factorises to $\left(x + a\right)^{2}$
  - E.g.  $x^{2} + 6 x + 9  =  \left(x + 3\right)^{2}$

> **Exam Hint**
> A common **mistake** in the exam is to divide **expressions** by numbers, e.g. $2x^{2}+4x+2$ becomes $x^{2}+2x+1$ (which is incorrect).
> 
> This can only be done with equations.
> 
> e.g. $2x^{2}+4x+2=0$ becomes $x^{2}+2x+1=0$ (dividing "both sides" by 2).

> **Worked Example**
> Factorise  $-8x^{2}+100x-48$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Spot the common factor of -4 and factorise it out*
> 
> $- 8 x^{2} + 100 x - 48 = - 4 \left(2 x^{2} - 25 x + 12\right)$
> 
> > *Check to see if the quadratic in the bracket will factorise using *$b^{2}-4ac$
> 
> $\begin{aligned} & & \left(- 25\right)^{2} - \left(4 \times 2 \times 12\right) \\ & = & 625 - 96 \\ & = & 529\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *529 is a square number (23*<sup>*2*</sup>*) so the expression will factorise*
> 
> > *Factorise *$2x^{2}-25x+12$
> 
> > *We require a pair of numbers which multiply to **ac**, and sum to **b*
> 
> $a\timesc=2\times12=24$
> 
> > *The only numbers which multiply to 24 and sum to -25 are*
> 
> *-24 and -1*
> 
> > *Split the *$-25x$* term into *$-24x-x$
> 
> $\begin{aligned} & & 2 x^{2} - 24 x - x + 12\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Group and factorise the first two terms, using *$2x$* as the common factor*
> *Group and factorise the last two terms using *$-1$* as the common factor*
> 
> $\begin{aligned} & & 2 x \left(x - 12\right) - 1 \left(x - 12\right)\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *These factorised terms now have a common factor of *$\left(x - 12\right)$*, so this can be factorised out*
> 
> $\left(2 x - 1\right) \left(x - 12\right)$
> 
> > *Recall that -4 was factorised out at the start*
> 
> $- 8 x^{2} + 100 x - 48 = - 4 \left(2 x^{2} - 25 x + 12\right) = - 4 \left(2 x - 1\right) \left(x - 12\right)$
> 
> $-4(2x-1)(x-12)$

title: Difference Of Two Squares
bodyMd:
# Difference Of Two Squares

## Difference Of Two Squares

> **Spec point** — `2.2F`

## Difference of two squares

### What is the difference of two squares?

- When a "squared" quantity is subtracted from another "squared" quantity, you get the **difference** of** two squares**

  - For example:
  
    - *a*<sup>2</sup> - *b*<sup>2</sup>
    - 9<sup>2</sup> - 5<sup>2</sup>
    - (*x* + 1)<sup>2</sup> - (*x* - 4)<sup>2</sup>
    - 4*m*<sup>2</sup> - 25*n*<sup>2</sup>, which is (2*m*)<sup>2</sup> - (5*n*)<sup>2</sup>

### How do I factorise the difference of two squares?

- ***a***<sup>**2**</sup>** - *****b***<sup>**2**</sup>** factorises to (*****a *****+ *****b*****)(*****a *****- *****b*****)**

  - This can be shown by expanding the brackets
  
    - $\left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right) = a^{2} - a b + b a - b^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2}$
  - The brackets can swap order
  
    - ***a***<sup>**2**</sup>** - *****b***<sup>**2**</sup>** = (*****a *****+ *****b*****)(*****a *****- *****b*****) = (*****a *****- *****b*****)(*****a *****+ *****b*****)**
    - (but terms inside a bracket cannot swap order)
- For example, $x^{2} - 9 = \left(x + 3\right) \left(x - 3\right)$

  - This** is the same** as $\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)$
  - But** not the same **as $\left(3 + x\right) \left(3 - x\right)$
  
    - which expands to $9-x^{2}$

### How can the difference of two squares be made harder?

- You may find it used with **numbers**

  - 7<sup>2</sup> - 3<sup>2</sup> = (7+3) (7-3) = (10) (4) = 40
- You can use a combination of **square numbers** and **squared variables**

  - 4*m*<sup>2</sup> - 9*n*<sup>2</sup> = (2*m*)<sup>2</sup> - (3*n*)<sup>2</sup> = (2*m* + 3*n*)(2*m* - 3*n*)
- You can use **other powers** which can be written as a **difference of two squares**

  - *r*<sup>8</sup> - *t*<sup>6</sup> =  (*r*<sup>4</sup>)<sup>2</sup> - (*t*<sup>3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = (*r*<sup>4 </sup>+ *t*<sup>3</sup>) (*r*<sup>4 </sup>- *t*<sup>3</sup>)
- You can use the difference of two squares **more than once **to** fully factorise** expressions

  - *a*<sup>4</sup> - *b*<sup>4</sup> = (*a*<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup> - (*b*<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = (*a*<sup>2 </sup>+ *b*<sup>2</sup>) (*a*<sup>2 </sup>- *b*<sup>2</sup>) = (*a*<sup>2 </sup>+ *b*<sup>2</sup>)(*a*<sup> </sup>+ *b*)(*a*<sup> </sup>- *b*)
- You may also need to **take out a common factor first**

  - $2 x^{2} - 18 = 2 \left(x^{2} - 9\right)$ giving $2 \left(x + 3\right) \left(x - 3\right)$
  
    - The 2 comes out in front

### Can I use the difference of two squares to expand?

- Using the difference of two squares to **expand** is **quicker** than expanding  double brackets and collecting like terms
- Brackets of the form **(*****a *****+ *****b*****)(*****a *****- *****b*****) expand to *****a***<sup>**2**</sup>** - *****b***<sup>**2**</sup>

  - For example $\left(2 x + 3\right) \left(2 x - 3\right)$ expands to  $4x^{2}-9$

> **Exam Hint**
> The difference between two squares is often the "trick" required to complete a harder algebraic question in the exam.
> 
> Learning to spot it can help speed up your working.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Factorise  $9x^{2}-16$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Recognise that *$9x^{2}$* and *$16$* are both squared terms *
> 
> > *Therefore you can factorise using the difference of two squares*
> 
> > *Rewrite as a difference of two squared terms*
> 
> $9 x^{2} - 16 = \left(3 x\right)^{2} - \left(4\right)^{2}$
> 
> > *Use the rule *$a^{2} - b^{2} = \left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right)$
> 
> **Final answer:** $(3x+4)(3x-4)$** **
> 
> (b) Factorise $4r^{2}-t^{4}$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Recognise that *$4r^{2}$* and *$t^{4}$* are both squared terms *
> 
> > *Therefore you can factorise using the difference of two squares*
> 
> > *Rewrite as a difference of two squared terms*
> 
> $4 r^{2} - t^{4} = \left(2 r\right)^{2} - \left(t^{2}\right)^{2}$
> 
> > *Use the rule *$a^{2} - b^{2} = \left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right)$
> 
> $(2r+t^{2})(2r-t^{2})$
> 
> (c) Factorise $2y^{2}-50$
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *This does not appear to be in the form *$a^{2}-b^{2}$
> 
> > *There is a common factor of 2, so take this factor out*
> 
> $2 \left(y^{2} - 25\right)$
> 
> > *You can now see *$y^{2}-25$* which has the form *$y^{2}-5^{2}$
> 
> > *Use the rule *$a^{2} - b^{2} = \left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right)$
> 
> $y^{2} - 25 = \left(y + 5\right) \left(y - 5\right)$
> 
> > *Now multiply this answer by 2 (leaving the 2 on the outside)*
> 
> $2 \left(y + 5\right) \left(y - 5\right)$

title: Factorising by Grouping
bodyMd:
# Factorising by Grouping

## Factorising by Grouping

> **Spec point** — `2.2F`

## Factorising by grouping

### How do I factorise expressions with a common bracket?

- Look at the expression  3*x*(*t* + 4) + 2(*t* + 4)

  - Both terms have a **common** **bracket**, (*t *+ 4)
  - The whole bracket, (*t* + 4), can be "taken out" like a common factor:
  
    - (*t* + 4)(3*x* + 2)
- This is like factorising 3*xy *+ 2*y* to get *y*(3*x *+ 2)

  - *y* represents (*t* + 4) above

#### How do I factorise by grouping?

- Some questions may require you to** form a common bracket yourself**

  - For example  *xy* + 3*x* + 5*y* + 15
  
    - The first two terms have a common factor of *x*
    - The second two terms have a common factor of 5
  - Factorising fully the **first pair** of terms, and the** last pair** of terms:
  
    - *x*(*y *+ 3) + 5(*y *+ 3)
  - You can now spot a common bracket of (*y *+ 3)
  
    - (*y *+ 3)(*x *+ 5)

- This is called** factorising by grouping**

#### Does it matter what order I group in?

- You can often** rearrange terms **to factorise in a** different order**

  - Rewriting the same example, *xy* + 3*x* + 5*y* + 15,  but in a different order:
  
    - *xy* + 5*y* + 3*x* + 15
    - The first pair of terms have a common factor of *y*
    - The second pair of terms have a common factor of 3
  - Factorising gives  *y*(*x *+ 5) + 3(*x *+ 5)
  
    - You can now spot a common bracket, this time of (*x* + 5)
  - (*x*+5)(*y*+3)
  
    - This gives the **same result** as found previously
- Some rearrangements **cannot **be factorised as "first pair" then "second pair"

  - For example, rewriting the above example as *xy* + 15 + 3*x* + 5*y*

> **Exam Hint**
> Once you have factorised something, expand it by hand to check your answer is correct.

> **Worked Example**
> Factorise *ab *+ 3*b *+* *2*a *+ 6.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Method 1**
> 
> > *Notice that **ab** and 3**b** have a common factor of **b*
> *Notice that 2**a** and 6 have a common factor of 2*
> 
> > *Factorise the first two terms, using **b** as a common factor*
> 
> **b(a ***+ 3)** **+*** ***2***a ***+ 6 *
> 
> > *Factorise the second two terms, using 2 as a common factor *
> 
> **b(a ***+ 3)** **+*** ***2(***a ***+ 3) *
> 
> > *(**a **+ 3) is a common bracket *
> *We can now factorise out the bracket (**a** + 3)*
> 
> **Final answer:** **(****a**** + 3)(****b**** + 2)**
> 
> **Method 2**
> 
> > *Notice that **ab** and 2**a** have a common factor of **a*
> *Notice that 3**b** and 6 have a common factor of 3*
> 
> > *Rewrite the expression, grouping these terms together *
> 
> **ab ***+ 2***a ***+ 3***b ***+ 6*
> 
> > *Factorise the first two terms, using **a** as a common factor *
> 
> **a***(***b*** + 2) + 3***b*** + 6*
> 
> > *Factorise the second two terms, using 3 as a common factor *
> 
> **a***(***b*** + 2) + 3(***b*** + 2) *
> 
> > *(**b **+ 2) is a common bracket*
> * We can now factorise out the bracket (**b** + 2)*
> 
> **Final answer:** **(****b**** + 2)(****a**** + 3)**

title: Factorising Harder Quadratics
bodyMd:
# Factorising Harder Quadratics

## Factorising Harder Quadratics

> **Spec point** — `2.2B`

## Factorising harder quadratics

### How do I factorise a quadratic expression where  a ≠ 1  in ax<sup>2</sup> + bx + c?

#### Method 1: Factorising by grouping

- This is shown most easily through an example: factorising $4x^{2}-25x-21$
- We need a **pair of numbers** that, for $ax^{2}+bx+c$

  - both **multiply **to give *ac*
  
    - *ac* in this case is 4 × -21 = -84
  - and both **add **to give *b*
  
    - *b* in this case is -25
  - -28 and +3 satisfy these conditions
  - **Rewrite **the middle term using -28*x* and +3*x*
  
    - $4x^{2}-28x+3x-21$
  - **Group **and fully **factorise **the** first two terms**, using 4*x* as the common factor
  - and **group **and fully **factorise **the **last two terms**, using 3 as the common factor
  
    - $4 x \left(x - 7\right) + 3 \left(x - 7\right)$
  - These terms now have a **common factor** of $\left(x - 7\right)$
  
    - This **whole bracket** can be factorised out
    - This gives the answer $\left(x - 7\right) \left(4 x + 3\right)$

#### Method 2: Factorising using a grid

- Use the same example: factorising $4x^{2}-25x-21$
- We need a **pair of numbers** that for $ax^{2}+bx+c$

  - **multiply **to give *ac*
  
    - *ac* in this case is 4 × -21 = -84
  - and **add **to give *b*
  
    - *b* in this case is -25
  - -28 and +3 satisfy these conditions
  - Write the quadratic expression in a **grid **
  
    - (as if you had used a grid to expand the brackets)
    - splitting the middle term up as -28*x* and +3*x *(either order)
  - The grid works by multiplying the row and column headings, to give a product in the boxes in the middle

|   |   |   |
|---|---|---|
|   | 4*x*<sup>2</sup> | -28*x* |
|   | +3*x* | -21 |

- Write a heading for the first row, using 4*x* as the highest common factor of 4*x*<sup>2</sup> and -28*x*

|   |   |   |
|---|---|---|
| **4*****x*** | 4*x*<sup>2</sup> | -28*x* |
|   | +3*x* | -21 |

- You can then use this to find the headings for the columns, e.g. “What does 4*x* need to be multiplied by to give 4*x*<sup>2</sup>?”

|   | ***x*** | **-7** |
|---|---|---|
| **4*****x*** | 4*x*<sup>2</sup> | -28*x* |
|   | +3*x* | -21 |

- We can then fill in the remaining row heading using the same idea, e.g. “What does *x* need to be multiplied by to give +3*x*?”

|   | ***x*** | **-7** |
|---|---|---|
| **4*****x*** | 4*x*<sup>2</sup> | -28*x* |
| **+3** | +3*x* | -21 |

- We can now read off the brackets from the column and row headings:

  - $\left(x - 7\right) \left(4 x + 3\right)$

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Factorise $6x^{2}-7x-3$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *We will factorise by grouping*
> 
> > *We need two numbers that:*
> 
> *multiply to 6 × -3 = -18*
> *and sum to -7*
> 
> *-9, and +2*
> 
> > *Split the middle term up using these values*
> 
> *6***x***<sup>2</sup>** + 2***x ***- 9***x*** - 3*
> 
> > *Factorise 2**x** out of the first two terms*
> 
> *2***x***(3***x*** + 1) - 9***x*** - 3*
> 
> > *Factorise -3 of out the last two terms*
> 
> *2***x***(3***x*** + 1) - 3(3***x*** + 1)*
> 
> > *These have a common factor of (3**x** + 1) which can be factorised out*
> 
> **Final answer:** **(3****x**** + 1)(2****x**** - 3)**
> 
> (b) Factorise $10x^{2}+9x-7$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *We will factorise using a grid*
> 
> > *We need two numbers that:*
> 
> *multiply to 10 × -7 = -70*
> *and sum to +9*
> 
> *-5, and +14*
> 
> > *Use these values to split the 9**x** term and write in a grid*
> 
> |   |   |   |
> |---|---|---|
> |   | *10***x***<sup>2</sup>* | *-5***x** |
> |   | *+14***x** | *-7* |
> 
> > *Write a heading using a common factor of 5**x** from the first row*
> 
> |   |   |   |
> |---|---|---|
> | ***5*******x**** | *10***x***<sup>2</sup>* | *-5***x** |
> |   | *+14***x** | *-7* |
> 
> > *Work out the headings for the rows, e.g. “What does 5**x** need to be multiplied by to make 10**x*<sup>*2*</sup>*?”*
> 
> |   | ***2*******x**** | ***-1*** |
> |---|---|---|
> | ***5*******x**** | *10***x***<sup>2</sup>* | *-5***x** |
> |   | *+14***x** | *-7* |
> 
> > *Repeat for the heading for the remaining row, e.g. “What does 2**x** need to be multiplied by to make +14**x**?”*
> 
> |   | ***2*******x**** | ***-1*** |
> |---|---|---|
> | ***5*******x**** | *10***x***<sup>2</sup>* | *-5***x** |
> | ***+7*** | *+14***x** | *-7* |
> 
> > *Read off the brackets from the column and row headings*
> 
> **Final answer:** **(2****x**** - 1)(5****x**** + 7)**

title: Factorising Out Terms
bodyMd:
# Factorising Out Terms

## Basic Factorising

> **Spec point** — `2.2D`

## Basic factorising

### What is factorisation?

- A **factorised **expression is one written as the **product** (**multiplication**) of two, or more, terms (**factors**)

  - 3(*x*  + 2) is factorised
  
    - It is 3 × (*x*  + 2)
  - 3*x*  + 6* * is **not** factorised
  - 3*xy * is factorised
  
    - It is 3 × *x*  × *y*
  - Numbers can also be factorised
  
    - 12 = 2 x 2 x 3
- In algebra, factorisation is the **reverse** of **expanding brackets**

  - It's putting it into brackets, rather than removing brackets

### How do I factorise two terms?

- To factorise 12*x*<sup>2</sup> + 18*x *

  - Find the highest common factor of the **number **parts
  
    - 6
  - Find the highest common factor of the **algebra** parts
  
    - *x*
  - Multiply both to get the overall **highest common factor**
  
    - 6*x*
  - 12*x*<sup>2</sup> + 18*x * is the same as 6*x * × 2*x*  + 6*x*  × 3
  
    - Using the highest common factor
  - **Take out** the highest common factor
  
    - Write it **outside** a set of **brackets**
    - Put the remaining terms, 2*x * + 3,  inside the brackets
  - This gives the answer
  
    - 6*x *(2*x*  + 3)
- To factorise an expression containing multiple variables, e.g. 2*a*<sup>3</sup>*b* - 4*a*<sup>*2*</sup>*b*<sup>2</sup>

  - Use the same approach as above
  - Find the highest common factor of the **number **parts
  
    - 2
  - Find the highest common factor of the **algebra** parts
  
    - *a* and *b* appear in both terms
    - The highest common factor of *a*<sup>3</sup> and *a*<sup>2</sup> is *a*<sup>2</sup>
    - The highest common factor of *b* and *b*<sup>2</sup> is *b*
    - *a*<sup>*2*</sup>*b*
  - Multiply both to get the overall **highest common factor**
  
    - 2*a*<sup>2</sup>*b*
  - 2*a*<sup>3</sup>*b* - 4*a*<sup>*2*</sup>*b*<sup>2</sup>* * is the same as 2*a*<sup>2</sup>*b * × a  -  2*a*<sup>2</sup>*b*  × 2*b*
  
    - Using the highest common factor
  - **Take out** the highest common factor
  
    - Write it **outside** a set of **brackets**
    - Put the remaining terms, *a - 2b*,  inside the brackets
  - This gives the answer
  
    - 2*a*<sup>2</sup>*b *(*a* - 2*b*)

> **Exam Hint**
> In the exam, check that your factorisation is correct by **expanding **the brackets.
> 
> **Factorise** means factorise **fully.**
> 
> *x *(6*x  *+ 10) is not fully factorised but 2*x *(3*x *+ 5) is.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Factorise 5*x* + 15
> **Answer:**
> 
> *Find the highest common factor of 5 and 15*
> 
> *5*
> 
> > *There is no **x** in the second term, so no highest common factor in **x**  is needed*
> *Think of each term as 5 × something*
> 
> *5 × ***x*** + 5 × 3*
> 
> > *Take out the 5 and put **x ** + 3 in brackets*
> 
> **Final answer:** **5(****x **** + 3)**
> 
> (b) Factorise fully 30*x*<sup>2</sup> - 24*x*
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> *Find the highest common factor of 30 and 24*
> 
> *6*
> 
> > *Find the highest common factor of **x*<sup>*2*</sup>*  and **x*
> 
> **x**
> 
> > *Find the overall highest common factor by multiplying these together*
> 
> *6***x**
> 
> > *Think of each term as 6**x**  × something*
> 
> *6***x***  × 5***x***  - 6***x***  × 4*
> 
> > *Take out the 6**x ** and put 5**x**  - 4 in brackets*
> 
> **Final answer:** **6****x ****(5****x **** - 4)**
> 
> (c) Factorise fully 5*x*<sup>4</sup>y + 25*x*<sup>*3*</sup>*y*<sup>*3*</sup>
> 
> **Answer**:
>
