> *Find the highest common factor of 5 and 25*
> 
> *5*
> 
> > *Find the highest common factor of **x*<sup>*4*</sup>*  and **x*<sup>*3*</sup>
> 
> **x***<sup>3</sup>*
> 
> > *Find the highest common factor of **y** and **y*<sup>*3*</sup>
> 
> **y**
> 
> > *Find the overall highest common factor by multiplying these together*
> 
> *5***x***<sup>*3*</sup>***y**
> 
> > *Think of each term as 5**x*<sup>*3*</sup>*y**  × something*
> 
> *5***x***<sup>*3*</sup>***y***  × ***x***  + 5***x***<sup>*3*</sup>***y***  × 5***y***<sup>2</sup>*<sup> </sup>
> 
> > *Take out the 5**x*<sup>*3*</sup>*y ** and put **x**  + 5**y*<sup>*2*</sup>* in brackets*
> 
> **Final answer:** **5****x**<sup>**3**</sup>**y**** ****(****x****  + 5****y**<sup>**2**</sup>**)**

title: Factorising Simple Quadratics
bodyMd:
# Factorising Simple Quadratics

## Factorising Simple Quadratics

> **Spec point** — `2.2F`

## Factorising simple quadratics

### What is a quadratic expression?

- A **quadratic expression** is in the form:

  - *ax*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c* (where *a* ≠ 0)
- If there are any **higher powers** of *x* (like *x*<sup>3</sup> say) then it is **not **a quadratic

### How do I factorise quadratics by inspection?

- This is shown most easily through an example: factorising $x^{2}-2x-8$

- We need a **pair of numbers** that for $x^{2}+bx+c$

  - **multiply** to give *c*
  
    - which in this case is -8
  - and **add** to give *b*
  
    - which in this case is -2
  - +2 and -4 satisfy these conditions
  
    - 2 × (-4) = -8  and  2 + (-4) = -2
  - **Write** these numbers in a **pair of brackets** like this:
  
    - $\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 4\right)$

### How do I factorise quadratics by grouping?

- This is shown most easily through an example: factorising $x^{2}-2x-8$

- We need a **pair of numbers** that for $x^{2}+bx+c$

  - **multiply** to give *c*
  
    - which in this case is -8
  - and **add** to give* b*
  
    - which in this case is -2
  - +2 and -4 satisfy these conditions
  
    - 2 × (-4) = -8  and  2 + (-4) = -2
  - **Rewrite** the middle term by using +2*x* and -4*x*
  
    - $x^{2}+2x-4x-8$
  - **Group** and **factorise** the **first two terms**, using *x* as the common factor
  - and **group** and **factorise** the **last two terms**, using -4 as the common factor
  
    - $x \left(x + 2\right) - 4 \left(x + 2\right)$
  - Note that these both now have a **common factor** of (*x* + 2) so this **whole** **bracket** can be factorised out
  
    - $\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 4\right)$

### How do I factorise quadratics using a grid?

- This is shown most easily through an example: factorising $x^{2}-2x-8$

- We need a **pair of numbers** that for $x^{2}+bx+c$

  - **multiply** to give *c*
  
    - which in this case is -8
  - and **add** to give* b*
  
    - which in this case is -2
  - +2 and -4 satisfy these conditions
  
    - 2 × (-4) = -8  and  2 + (-4) = -2
  - Write the quadratic equation in a **grid** (as if you had used a grid to expand the brackets)
  
    - splitting the middle term as +2*x* and -4*x*
- The grid works by multiplying the row and column headings, to give a product in the boxes in the middle

|   |   |   |
|---|---|---|
|   | *x*<sup>2</sup> | -4*x* |
|   | +2*x* | -8 |

- Write a heading for the first row, using *x* as the highest common factor of *x*<sup>2</sup> and -4*x*

|   |   |   |
|---|---|---|
| ***x*** | *x*<sup>2</sup> | -4*x* |
|   | +2*x* | -8 |

- You can then use this to find the headings for the columns

  - e.g. “What does *x* need to be multiplied by to give *x*<sup>2</sup>?”
  - and “What does *x* need to be multiplied by to give -4*x*?”

|   | ***x*** | **-4** |
|---|---|---|
| ***x*** | *x*<sup>2</sup> | -4*x* |
|   | +2*x* | -8 |

- We can then fill in the remaining row heading using the same idea

  - e.g. “What does *x* need to be multiplied by to give +2*x*?”
  - or “What does -4 need to be multiplied by to give -8?”

|   | ***x*** | **-4** |
|---|---|---|
| ***x*** | *x*<sup>2</sup> | -4*x* |
| **+2** | +2*x* | -8 |

- We can now read off the factors from the column and row headings

  - $\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 4\right)$

### Which method should I use for factorising simple quadratics?

- The first method, by **inspection**, is by far the **quickest**

  - So this is recommended in an exam for simple quadratics (where *a *= 1)
- However some students find the other methods helpful

  - So you may want to learn at least one of them too

> **Exam Hint**
> As a check, expand your answer and make sure you get the same expression as the one you were trying to factorise.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Factorise $x^{2}-4x-21$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *We will factorise by inspection*
> 
> > *We need two numbers that multiply to give -21, and sum to give -4*
> *+3 and -7 satisfy this*
> 
> $3 \times ( - 7 ) = - 21$
> 
$> 3 + ( - 7 ) = - 4$
> 
> > *Write down the brackets*
> 
> **Final answer:** ** (****x**** + 3)(****x**** - 7)**
> 
> (b) Factorise $x^{2}-5x+6$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *We will factorise by splitting the middle term and grouping*
> 
> > *We need two numbers that multiply to 6, and sum to -5*
> *-3 and -2 satisfy this*
> 
> $( - 3 ) \times ( - 2 ) = 6$
> 
$> ( - 3 ) + ( - 2 ) = - 5$
> 
> > *Split the middle term*
> 
> **x***<sup>2</sup>** - 2***x*** - 3***x*** + 6*
> 
> > *Factorise **x** out of the first two terms*
> 
> **x***(***x*** - 2) - 3***x*** +6*
> 
> > *Factorise -3 out of the last two terms*
> 
> **x***(***x*** - 2) - 3(***x*** - 2)*
> 
> > *These have a common factor of (**x** - 2) which can be factored out*
> 
> **Final answer:** **(****x**** - 2)(****x**** - 3)**
> 
> (c) Factorise $x^{2}-2x-24$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *We will factorise by using a grid*
> 
> > *We need two numbers that multiply to -24, and sum to -2*
> *+4, and -6 satisfy this*
> 
> $4 \times ( - 6 ) = - 24$
> 
$> 4 + ( - 6 ) = - 2$
> 
> > *Use these to split the -2**x** term and write in a grid*
> 
> |   |   |   |
> |---|---|---|
> |   | **x***<sup>2</sup>* | *+4***x** |
> |   | *-6***x** | *-24* |
> 
> > *Write a heading using a common factor for the first row*
> 
> |   |   |   |
> |---|---|---|
> | ****x**** | **x***<sup>2</sup>* | *+4***x** |
> | * * | *-6***x** | *-24* |
> 
> *Work out the headings for the rows*
> *“What does **x** need to be multiplied by to make **x*<sup>*2*</sup>*?”*
> *“What does **x** need to be multiplied by to make +4**x**?”*
> 
> | * * | ****x**** | ***+4*** |
> |---|---|---|
> | ****x**** | **x***<sup>2</sup>* | *+4***x** |
> | * * | *-6***x** | *-24* |
> 
> *Repeat for the heading for the remaining row*
> *“What does **x** need to be multiplied by to make -6**x**?”*
> *(Or “What does +4 need to be multiplied by to make -24?”)*
> 
> | * * | ****x**** | ***+4*** |
> |---|---|---|
> | ****x**** | **x***<sup>2</sup>* | *+4***x** |
> | ***-6*** | *-6***x** | *-24* |
> 
> > *Read off the factors from the column and row headings*
> 
> **Final answer:** **(****x**** + 4)(****x**** - 6)**

title: Forming Equations from Words
bodyMd:
# Forming Equations from Words

## Forming & Solving Equations

> **Spec point** — `2.4B`

## Forming linear equations

### How do I form expressions from words?

- You can turn common** phrases** into expressions

  - **Use *****x***** **to represent an** unknown** value | 2 less than "something" | $x-2$ |
  |---|---|
  | Double "something" | $2x$ |
  | 5 lots of "something" | $5x$ |
  | 3 more than "something" | $x+3$ |
  | Half of "something" | $\frac{1}{2}x\mathrm{or}\frac{x}{2}$ |
- Common words indicating basic operations are:

  - **Addition**: sum, total, more than, increase
  - **Subtraction**: difference, less than, decrease
  - **Multiplication**: product, lots of, times as many, double, triple
  - **Division**: shared, split, grouped, halved, quartered
- **Brackets** help keep the **order** correct

  - "something" add 1, then multiplied by 3
  
    - $(x+1)\times3$ which simplifies to $3(x+1)$
  - Compare this to "something" multiplied by 3, then add 1
  
    - $x\times3+1$ which simplifies to $3x+1$
- You may have to **choose** which unknown to call *x*

  - If Adam is 10 years **younger** than Barry, then Barry is 10 years **older** than Adam
  
    - Either represent Adam's age as $x-10$ and Barry's age as $x$
    - Or represent Adam's age as $x$ and Barry's age as $x+10$
  - If Adam's age is **half **of Barry's age, then Barry's age is **double** Adam's age
  
    - So if Adam's age is $x$ then Barry's age is $2x$
    - This makes the algebra easier (rather than using $x$ for Barry's age and $\frac{1}{2}x$ for Adam's age)

### How do I form equations?

- An** equation** is a statement with an** equals** sign that can be **solved**
- Try to put in the phrase "**is equal to**" to see where the equals goes

  - Lisa's age is double Aisha's age and the sum of their ages** **is ("is equal to") 27
  
    - Represent Aisha's age as $x$ and Lisa's age is $2x$
    - The equation is $2x+x=27$
  - When solving, always give the answer in context
  
    - $3x=27$ so $x=9$
    - In context: "Lisa is 18 years old and Aisha is 9 years old"
- Sometimes you might have** two** unknown values (*x*  and *y*)

  - Use the information to form two **simultaneous** equations

> **Worked Example**
> A flowerbed has flowers of three different colours: red, yellow and purple.
> The number of yellow flowers is three times the number of red flowers.
> The number of purple flowers is 5 more than the number of yellow flowers.
> 
> If the difference between the number of purple flowers and red flowers is 29, find the number of yellow flowers.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Let the number of red flowers be** x*
> 
> $x$* red flowers*
> 
> > *Multiply this by 3 to get the number of yellow flowers*
> 
> $3x$* yellow flowers*
> 
> > *Add 5 to the previous result to get the number of purple flowers*
> 
> $3x+5$* purple flowers*
> 
> > *Find the difference between the number of purple and red flowers (purple subtract red, as purple is larger)*
> 
> $3x+5-x$
> 
> *Set the difference equal to 29*
> 
> $3x+5-x=29$
> 
> *Simplify the left-hand side (3**x **- **x **= 2**x**)*
> 
> $2x+5=29$
> 
> *Solve the equation (subtract 5 then divide by 2)*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 x & = & 29 - 5 \\ 2 x & = & 24 \\ x & = & \frac{24}{2} \\ x & = & 12\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *This is not the answer to the question asked*
> *The number of yellow flowers is 3**x** so multiply this answer by 3*
> 
> **Final answer:** **There are 36 yellow flowers**

title: Solving Linear Equations
bodyMd:
# Solving Linear Equations

## Solving Linear Equations

> **Spec point** — `2.4B`

## Solving linear equations

### What are linear equations?

- A** linear equation** is one that can be written in the **form** $ax+b=c$

  - $a,b,$ and $c$* *are **numbers** and $x$is the **variable**
  
    - 2*x* + 3 = 5
    - 3*x* + 4 = 1
    - *x* - 5 = -3
- The greatest power of *x *is 1

  - There are no terms like *x*<sup>2</sup>

### How do I solve linear equations?

- You need to use **operations** like adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing to get ***x*** on its **own**
- Any operation you do to **one side **of the **equation** must also be done to the **other side**
- For example, to solve  $2x+1=9$ look at the +1 on the left

  - Undo this by subtracting 1 from **both sides** and **simplifying**

$\begin{aligned}2 x + 1 & = & 9\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(- 1\right) \text{   }\end{aligned} \text{   } \begin{aligned} & & \text{   } \left(- 1\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}2 x & = & 8\end{aligned}$

- This equation is now **easier** to solve
- 2*x* is 2 × *x  *so undo this by dividing **both** sides by 2 and **simplifying**

$\begin{aligned}2 x & = & 8\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(\div 2\right) \text{   }\end{aligned} \text{   } \begin{aligned} & & \text{   } \left(\div 2\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 4\end{aligned}$

- The **solution** to the equation is *x* = 4
- Adding 1 was undone by subtracting 1
- Multiplying by 2 was undone by dividing by 2

  - **Addition** and **subtraction** are said to be **inverse **(opposite) operations
  - **Multiplication **and **division **are also **inverse** operations

### Does the order of steps matter?

- As long as each step is applied correctly, the order in which inverse operations are applied **does not matter**

  - Applying the operations in one order may be easier than another
- Consider $4x+8=12$

  - It is **easier **to **first subtract** 8 from both sides

$4x=4$

- **Then** **divide** both sides by 4

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 1\end{aligned}$

- If you want to first divide by 4, a common** mistake** is to write $x+8=3$

  - This is **incorrect** as 8 has not been divided by 4
  - You must divide **every term** by 4

$\begin{aligned}\frac{4 x}{4} + \frac{8}{4} & = & \frac{12}{4} \\ x + 2 & = & 3\end{aligned}$

- Then subtract 2 from both sides

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 1\end{aligned}$

### How do I solve linear equations with negative numbers?

- For example,  $2-3x=10$

  - Subtract 2 from both sides and simplify

$\begin{aligned}2 - 3 x & = & 10\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(- 2\right) \text{   }\end{aligned} \text{   } \begin{aligned} & & \text{   } \left(- 2\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}- 3 x & = & 8\end{aligned}$

- Then divide both sides by -3 and simplify

$\begin{aligned}- 3 x & = & 8\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & &  \left(\div - 3\right) \text{   }\end{aligned} \text{   } \begin{aligned} & & \text{   } \left(\div - 3\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}x & = & - \frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}$

- Some people prefer to write $2-3x=10$ as $-3x+2=10$, which is equivalent

  - You then subtract 2 and divide by -3 as before

> **Exam Hint**
> Substitute your answer back into the original equation to check you got it right!

> **Worked Example**
> Solve the equation
> 
> $9-7x=5$
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Subtract 9 from both sides of the equation*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}- 7 x & = & - 4\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Divide both sides by -7*
> *Remember that a negative divided by a negative will result in a positive number*
> 
> $x=\frac{-4}{-7}$
> 
> $x=\frac{4}{7}$

### How do I solve linear equations with brackets?

- If a linear equation involves brackets, **expand **the brackets first
- For example, solve $2 \left(x - 3\right) = 10$

  - Expand the brackets

$2x-6=10$

- Then solve as shown previously

  - Add 6 then divide by 2

$\begin{aligned}2 x & = & 16 \\ x & = & 8\end{aligned}$

- **Expanding** brackets** first** will always work, but you can also divide first

  - Dividing **both **sides of $2 \left(x - 3\right) = 10$ by 2 gives $\left(x - 3\right) = 5$
  
    - which gives $x=8$
  - This method works but can lead to harder **fractions**

### How do I solve linear equations with fractions?

- If a linear equation contains** fractions**, **multiply** **both sides **by the **lowest common** **denominator**
- For example,  $\frac{x}{5}+4=\frac{9}{2}$

  - The lowest common denominator of 5 and 2 is 10
  - Multiply **all terms** on both sides by 10

$\begin{aligned}\left(10 \times \frac{x}{5}\right) + \left(10 \times 4\right) & = & 10 \times \frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{10 x}{5} + 40 & = & \frac{90}{2}\end{aligned}$

- **Simplify **the fractions

$\begin{aligned}2 x + 40 & = & 45\end{aligned}$

- Now solve as before, by subtracting 40, then dividing by 2

$\begin{aligned}2 x & = & 5 \\ x & = & \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$

- Unless the question specifies otherwise, you can leave the answer like this

  - A** decimal** or **mixed number** would also be **accepted**

#### What if the unknown is on the denominator?

- For example $\frac{4}{x-2}=3$

  - Multiply both sides of the equation by the denominator

$\frac{4}{x - 2} \times \left(x - 2\right) = 3 \left(x - 2\right)$

- Simplify the fractions, and expand any brackets

$4 = 3 \left(x - 2\right)$
4 equals 3 x minus 6

- Now solve as before, by adding 6 to both sides, then dividing by 3

$\begin{aligned}10 & = & 3 x \\ \frac{10}{3} & = & x\end{aligned}$

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Solve the equation
> 
> $5 \left(3 - 4 x\right) + 1 = 26$
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Expand the bracket*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}15 - 20 x + 1 & = & 26\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Simplify*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}16 - 20 x & = & 26\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *It can be helpful to consider 16 - 20**x** as -20**x** + 16*
> *Subtract 16 from both sides*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}- 20 x & = & 10\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Divide both sides by -20 and simplify*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{10}{- 20} \\ x & = & - \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$
> 
> $x=-\frac{1}{2}$
> 
> > *-0.5 is also accepted*
> 
> (b) Solve the equation
> 
> $\frac{5x}{4}=\frac{1}{2}$
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *The lowest common denominator of 4 and 2 is 4*
> *Multiply both sides by 4*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}4 \times \frac{5 x}{4} & = & 4 \times \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Simplify (cancel) the fractions*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}5 x & = & 2\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *To solve this equation, divide both sides by 5*
> 
> $x=\frac{2}{5}$

### How do I solve linear equations with x terms on both sides?

- **Collect the *****x***** terms **(or whichever variable is involved)** together on one side **

  - To do this, **remove all the *****x***** terms from one side**
  
    - It is easiest to remove the **smallest *****x***** term** to avoid negatives
- For example,  $4x-7=11+x$
- Remove the *x* term on the right-hand side, by subtracting *x* from both sides

$\begin{aligned}4 x - 7 & = & 11 + x\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(- x\right) \text{   } \left(- x\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}3 x - 7 & = & 11\end{aligned}$

- There are no longer any *x* terms on the right
- This now has the same form as previously seen

  - Solve by adding 7 then dividing by 3

$\begin{aligned}3 x - 7 & = & 11 \\ 3 x & = & 18 \\ x & = & 6\end{aligned}$

> **Worked Example**
> Solve the equation
> 
> $4-5x=6x-29$
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Remove the **x** terms from either side*
> *We will remove them from the left as -5**x **is smaller than 6**x*
> 
> > *Add 5**x** to both sides*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}4 & = & 11 x - 29\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Get 11**x **on its own by adding 29 to both sides*
> 
> $33=11x$
> 
> > *Divide both sides by 11 to find **x*
> 
> $3=x$
> 
> $x=3$

title: Deciding the Quadratic Method
bodyMd:
# Deciding the Quadratic Method

## Quadratic Equation Methods

> **Spec point** — `2.7B`

## Deciding the quadratic method

### When should I solve by factorisation?

- Use factorisation when the question asks to** solve by factorisation**

  - For example
  
    - part (a) Factorise 6*x*<sup>2</sup> + 7*x* – 3
    - part (b) Solve  6*x*<sup>2</sup> + 7*x* – 3 = 0
- Use factorisation when solving **two-term quadratic equations**

  - For example, solve *x*<sup>2</sup> – 4*x* = 0
  
    - Take out a **common factor **of *x* to get *x*(*x* – 4) = 0
    - So *x* = 0 and *x* = 4
  - For example, solve *x*<sup>2</sup> – 9 = 0
  
    - Use the **difference of two squares** to factorise it as (*x* + 3)(*x* – 3) = 0
    - So *x* = -3 and *x* = 3
    - (Or rearrange to *x*<sup>2</sup> = 9 and use ±√ to get *x* = ±3)
- Factorising can often be the **quickest** way to solve a quadratic equation

### When should I use the quadratic formula?

- Use the quadratic formula when the question says to leave solutions correct to** **a** given accuracy** (2 decimal places, 3 significant figures etc)

  - This is a hint that the equation will not factorise
- Use the quadratic formula when it may be **faster** **than factorising**

  - It's quicker to solve 36*x*<sup>2</sup> + 33*x* – 20 = 0 using the quadratic formula than by factorisation
- Use the quadratic formula **if in doubt**, as it **always works**

### When should I solve by completing the square?

- Use completing the square when part (a) of a question says to **complete the square** and part (b) says to use part (a) to solve the equation
- Use completing the square when making *x* the **subject of harder formulae** containing both *x*<sup>2</sup> and *x* terms

  - For example, make *x* the subject of the formula *x*<sup>2</sup> + 6*x* = *y*
  
    - Complete the square: (*x* + 3)<sup>2</sup> – 9 = *y*
    - Add 9 to both sides: (*x *+ 3)<sup>2</sup> = *y* + 9
    - Take square roots and use ±:  $x+3=\pm\sqrt{y+9}$
    - Subtract 3:  $x=-3\pm\sqrt{y+9}$
- Completing the square **always works**

  - But it's not always quick or easy to do

> **Exam Hint**
> - If your calculator solves quadratic equations, use it to check your solutions
> - If the solutions on your calculator are whole numbers or fractions (with no square roots), this means the quadratic equation does factorise

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Solve $x^{2}-7x+2=0$, giving your answers correct to 2 decimal places.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> *“Correct to 2 decimal places” suggests using the quadratic formula*
> *Substitute **a** = 1, **b** = -7 and **c** = 2 into the formula*
> *Put brackets around any negative numbers*
> 
> $x = \frac{- \left(- 7\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(- 7\right)^{2} - 4 \times 1 \times 2}}{2 \times 1}$
> 
> > *Use a calculator to find each solution *
> 
> **x*** = 6.70156… or 0.2984...*
> 
> > *Round your final answers to 2 decimal places*
> 
> **x**** = 6.70  or** **x**** = 0.30** **(2 d.p.)**
> 
> (b) Solve $16x^{2}-82x+45=0$.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> **Method 1**
> *If you cannot spot the factorisation, use the quadratic formula*
> *Substitute** a** = 16, **b** = -82 and **c **= 45 into the formula*
> *Put brackets around any negative numbers*
> 
> $x = \frac{- \left(- 82\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(- 82\right)^{2} - 4 \times 16 \times 45}}{2 \times 16}$
> 
> > *Use a calculator to find each solution*
> 
> **Final answer:** **x**** = **$\frac{9}{2}$**  or ****x**** = **$\frac{5}{8}$
> 
> **Method 2**
> *If you do spot the factorisation, (2x – 9)(8x – 5), then use that method instead*
> 
> $\left(2 x - 9\right) \left(8 x - 5\right) = 0$
> 
> > *Set the first bracket equal to zero*
> 
> $2x-9=0$
> 
> > *Add 9 to both sides then divide by 2*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}2 x & = & 9 \\ x & = & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Set the second bracket equal to zero*
> 
> $8x-5=0$
> 
> > *Add 5 to both sides then divide by 8*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}8 x & = & 5 \\ x & = & \frac{5}{8}\end{aligned}$
> 
> **Final answer:** **x**** = **$\frac{9}{2}$**  or ****x**** = **$\frac{5}{8}$
> 
> (c) By writing $x^{2}+6x+5$ in the form $\left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$, solve $x^{2}+6x+5=0$
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *This question wants you to complete the square first*
> *Find **p** (by halving the middle number)*
> 
> $p=\frac{6}{2}=3$
> 
> > *Write **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* + 6**x** as (**x** + **p**)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **p*<sup>*2*</sup>
> 
> $\begin{aligned}x^{2} + 6 x & = & \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 3^{2} \\ & = & \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 9\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Replace **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* + 6**x **with (**x** + 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* – 9 in the equation*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}\left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 9 + 5 & = & 0 \\ \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 4 & = & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Now solve it*
> *Make **x** the subject of the equation (start by adding 4 to both sides)*
> 
> $\left(x + 3\right)^{2} = 4$
> 
> > *Take square roots of both sides (include a ± sign to get both solutions)*
> 
> $x+3=\pm\sqrt{4}=\pm2$
> 
> > *Subtract 3 from both sides*
> 
> $x=-3\pm2$
> 
> > *Find each solution separately using + first, then - second*
> 
> **Final answer:** **x**** = - 1  or  ****x**** = - 5**

title: Solving by Completing the Square
bodyMd:
# Solving by Completing the Square

## Solving by Completing the Square

> **Spec point** — `2.7B`

## Solving by completing the square

### How do I solve a quadratic equation by completing the square?

- To solve *x*<sup>2</sup> + *bx *+* c* = 0

  - **replace** the first two terms, ***x***<sup>**2**</sup>** + *****bx***, with **(*****x***** + *****p*****)**<sup>**2**</sup>** - *****p***<sup>**2**</sup> where ***p***** is half of *****b***
  - This is** completing the square**
  
    - *x*<sup>2</sup> + *bx *+* c* = 0 becomes (*x* + *p*)<sup>2</sup> - *p*<sup>2</sup> + *c *= 0
    - (where *p* is half of *b)*
  - rearrange this equation to **make *****x***** the subject** (using ±√)
- For example, solve *x*<sup>2</sup> + 10*x* + 9 = 0 by completing the square

  - *x*<sup>2</sup> + 10*x *becomes (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> - 5<sup>2</sup>
  - so* x*<sup>2</sup> + 10*x* + 9 = 0 becomes (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> - 5<sup>2 </sup>+ 9 = 0
  - make *x* the subject (using ±√)
  
    - (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> - 25<sup> </sup>+ 9 = 0
    - (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> = 16
    - *x* + 5 = ±√16
    - *x* + 5 = ±4
    - *x*  = -5 ±4
    - *x*  = -1 or *x*  = -9
- It also works with numbers that lead to **surds**

  - The answers found will be in **exact** (**surd**) form

> **Exam Hint**
> When making *x* the subject to find the solutions, don't expand the squared bracket back out again!
> 
> - Remember to use ±√ to get** two** solutions

### How do I solve by completing the square when there is a coefficient in front of the x<sup>2</sup> term?

- If the equation is *ax*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c* = 0 with a **number** (other than 1)  **in front of *****x***<sup>**2**</sup>

  - you can **divide both sides by *****a**** *first (before completing the square)
  
    - For example  3*x*<sup>2</sup> + 12*x* + 9 = 0
    - Divide both sides by 3
    
      - *x*<sup>2</sup> + 4*x* + 3 = 0
    - Complete the square on this easier equation
- This trick **only** works when completing the square to **solve **a quadratic equation

  - i.e. it has an "=0" on the right-hand side
- **Don't** do this when using completing the square to rewrite a **quadratic expression** in a new form

  - i.e. when there is no "=0"
  - For that, you must **factorise out** the *a* (but not divide by it)
  
    - $a x^{2} + b x + c = a \left[x^{2} + \frac{b}{a} x\right] + c$ and so on

### How does completing the square link to the quadratic formula?

- The **quadratic formula** actually comes from **completing the square** to solve *ax*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c* = 0

  - *a*, *b* and *c* are left as letters when completing the square
  
    - This makes it as general as possible
- You can see hints of this when you solve quadratics

  - For example, solving *x*<sup>2</sup> + 10*x* + 9 = 0
  
    - by completing the square, (*x* + 5)<sup>2</sup> = 16 so *x*  = -5 ± 4 (as above)
    - by the quadratic formula,  $x=\frac{-10\pm\sqrt{64}}{2}=-5\pm\frac{8}{2}$ = -5 ± 4 (the same structure)

> **Worked Example**
> Solve $2x^{2}-8x-24=0$ by completing the square.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Divide both sides by 2 to make the quadratic start with **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* *
> 
> $x^{2}-4x-12=0$
> 
> > *Halve the middle number, -4, to get -2*
> *Replace the first two terms, **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* - 4**x**, with (**x** - 2)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - (-2)*<sup>*2*</sup>
> 
> $\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - \left(- 2\right)^{2} - 12 = 0$
> 
> > *Simplify the numbers*
> 
> $\begin{aligned}\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 4 - 12 & = & 0 \\ \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 16 & = & 0\end{aligned}$
> 
> > *Add 16 to both sides*
> 
> $\left(x - 2\right)^{2} = 16$
> 
> > *Take the square root of both sides*
> *Include the ± sign to get two solutions*
> 
> $x-2=\pm\sqrt{16}=\pm4$
> 
> > *Add 2 to both sides*
> 
> $x=2\pm4$
> 
> > *Work out each solution separately*
> 
> **Final answer:** **x**** = 6  or  ****x**** = -2**

title: Solving Quadratics by Factorising
bodyMd:
# Solving Quadratics by Factorising

## Solving Quadratics by Factorising

> **Spec point** — `2.7A`

## Solving quadratics by factorising

### How do I solve a quadratic equation using factorisation?

- **Rearrange** it into the form *ax*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c* = 0

  - Zero must be on one side
  - It is easier if you rearrange so that *a* is positive
- **Factorise** the quadratic and **solve** each bracket equal to zero

  - If (*x* + 4)(*x* - 1) = 0, then either *x* + 4 = 0 or *x* - 1 = 0
  
    - Because if two things multiply together to give zero,
    
      - then one or the other of them must be equal to zero
- To solve $\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 7\right) = 0$

  - …solve **first bracket = 0**:
  
    - *x* – 3 = 0
    - add 3 to both sides: x = 3
  - …and solve **second bracket = 0**
  
    - *x* + 7 = 0
    - subtract 7 from both sides: *x* = -7
  - The **two solutions** are *x* = 3 or *x* = -7
  
    - The solutions in this example are the numbers in the brackets, but with opposite signs

### What if there are numbers in front of the x's in the brackets?

- The process is **the same**

  - There's a bit more work to find the solutions
  - You can't just write down the answers by changing the signs
- To solve $\left(2 x - 3\right) \left(3 x + 5\right) = 0$

  - …solve **first bracket = 0**
  
    - 2*x* – 3 = 0
    - add 3 to both sides: 2*x* = 3
    - divide both sides by 2: *x* = $\frac{3}{2}$
  - …solve **second bracket = 0**
  
    - 3*x* + 5 = 0
    - subtract 5 from both sides: 3*x* = -5
    - divide both sides by 3: *x* = $-\frac{5}{3}$
  - The **two solutions** are *x* = $\frac{3}{2}$ or *x* = $-\frac{5}{3}$

### What if x is a factor?

- The process is **the same**

  - Just be sure to handle the *x* correctly
  - That '*x* as a factor' gives one of the solutions
- To solve $x \left(x - 4\right) = 0$

  - it may help to think of *x* as (*x* – 0) or (*x*)
  - …solve **first bracket = 0**
  
    - (*x*) = 0, so *x* = 0
  - …solve **second bracket = 0**
  
    - *x* – 4 = 0
    - add 4 to both sides: *x* = 4
  - The** two solutions** are* x* = 0 or *x *= 4
- It is a common **mistake** to divide (cancel) both sides by *x* at the beginning

  - If you do this you will **lose a solution** (the *x* = 0 solution)

> **Exam Hint**
> Your calculator might be able to solve quadratics. If it does, then you can use this to help you to factorise the quadratic.
> 
> For example, a calculator gives solutions to $6x^{2}+x-2=0$ as  $x=-\frac{2}{3}$  and $x=\frac{1}{2}$. You can rearrange these solutions to get zero on one side, $3x+2=0$ and $2x-1=0$. The left-hand side expressions are two factors,$6 x^{2} + x - 2 = \left(3 x  +  2\right) \left(2 x  -  1\right)$.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Solve $x^{2}+3x-10=0$ by factorising.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Factorise the left-hand side*
> 
> **(x*** – 2)(***x*** + 5)=0*
> 
> > *Set the first bracket equal to zero*
> 
> **x*** – 2 = 0*
> 
> > *Add 2 to both sides*
> 
> **x*** = 2*
> 
> > *Set the second bracket equal to zero*
> 
> **x*** + 5 = 0*
> 
> > *Subtract 5 from both sides*
> 
> **x*** = -5*
> 
> > *Write both solutions together using “or”*
> 
> **Final answer:** **x**** = 2 or ****x**** = -5**
> 
> (b) Solve $5x^{2}-x=0$ by factorising.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Factorise the left-hand side*
> 
> **x***(5***x*** - 1)=0*
> 
> > *Do not divide both sides by** x **(this will lose a solution at the end)*
> *Set the first bracket equal to zero*
> 
> *(x) = 0*
> 
> > *Solve this equation to find **x*
> 
> **x*** = 0*
> 
> > *Set the second bracket equal to zero*
> 
> *5***x*** - 1 = 0*
> 
> > *Add 1 to both sides*
> 
> *5***x*** = 1*
> 
> > *Divide both sides by 5*
> 
> **x*** = *$\frac{1}{5}$
> 
> > *Write both solutions together using “or”*
> 
> **Final answer:** **x**** = 0 or ****x**** =**** **$\frac{1}{5}$

title: The Quadratic Formula
bodyMd:
# The Quadratic Formula

## Quadratic Formula

> **Spec point** — `2.7B`

## Quadratic formula

### What is the quadratic formula?

- A **quadratic equation** has the form *ax*<sup>2</sup> + *bx* + *c* = 0 (where *a* ≠ 0)

  - you need "**= 0**" on one side
- The **quadratic formula** is a formula that gives both solutions to a quadratic equation:

$x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$

> **Exam Hint**
> Make sure the quadratic equation has "= 0" on the right-hand side, otherwise it needs rearranging first.

### How do I use the quadratic formula to solve a quadratic equation?

- Read off the **values** of *a*, *b* and *c* from the equation
- **Substitute** these into the formula

  - **Write** this line of working in the exam
  - Put **brackets** around any **negative numbers** being substituted in
- To solve 2*x*<sup>2</sup> - 8*x* - 3 = 0 using the quadratic formula:

  - *a* = 2, *b* = -8 and *c* = -3
  - $x = \frac{- \left(- 8\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(- 8\right)^{2} - 4 \times 2 \times \left(- 3\right)}}{2 \times 2}$
  - Either type this into a calculator or simplify by hand
  
    - Type it once using + for  ± then again using - for  ±
  - The **solutions** are *x* = 4.3452078... or *x* = -0.34520787....
  
    - To 3 **decimal places**: *x* = 4.345 or *x* = -0.345
    - To 3 **significant figures**: x = 4.35 or x = -0.345

> **Exam Hint**
> Always look for how the question wants you to leave your final answers. For example, correct to 2 decimal places.

### How do I write the solutions in an exact (surd) form?

- You may be asked to give answers in an **exact** (**surd**) form
- In the example above, work out the **number **under the **square root **sign

  - Be careful with negatives!
  
    - $\left(- 8\right)^{2} - 4 \times 2 \times \left(- 3\right) = 64 + 24 = 88$
  - Now square root this number and use **surd rules** to simplify
  
    - $\sqrt{88}=\sqrt{4\times22}=\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{22}=2\sqrt{22}$
  - **Substitute** this back into the formula and simplify
  
    - $x = \frac{8 \pm 2 \sqrt{22}}{4} = \frac{2 \left(4 \pm \sqrt{22}\right)}{4} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{22}}{2}$
    - The solutions in **exact** (**surd**) form are $x=\frac{4+\sqrt{22}}{2}$ or $x=\frac{4-\sqrt{22}}{2}$
- **Calculators** that can solve quadratics will give solutions in** exact** (**surd**) form

### What is the discriminant?

- The part of the formula under the square root (*b*<sup>2</sup> – 4*ac*) is called the **discriminant**
- The **sign** of this value tells you if there are 0, 1 or 2 solutions

  - If ***b***<sup>**2**</sup>** – 4*****ac***** > 0** (positive)
  
    - then there are 2 different solutions
  - If ***b***<sup>**2**</sup>** – 4*****ac***** = 0**
  
    - then there is only 1 solution
  - If ***b***<sup>**2**</sup>** – 4*****ac***** < 0** (negative)
  
    - then there are no real solutions
- If the discriminant is a **perfect square number** (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, …) then the quadratic expression can be factorised using integers

> **Exam Hint**
> You do not need to know about the discriminant for your exam. However, it might be useful to check whether a quadratic can be factorised using integers.

### Can I use my calculator to solve quadratic equations?

- If your calculator solves quadratic equations, use it to** check** your **final answers**

  - But a correct method and working must still be shown

> **Worked Example**
> Use the quadratic formula to find the solutions of the equation 3*x*<sup>2</sup> - 2*x* - 4 = 0.
> Give each solution as an exact value in its simplest form.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Write down the values of **a**, **b** and **c*
> 
> **a*** = 3, ***b*** = -2, ***c*** = -4*
> 
> > *Substitute these values into the quadratic formula, *$x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$
> *Put brackets around any negative numbers*
> 
> $x = \frac{- \left(- 2\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(- 2\right)^{2} - 4 \times 3 \times \left(- 4\right)}}{2 \times 3}$
> 
> > *Simplify the expressions*
> 
> $x=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{4+48}}{6}=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{52}}{6}$
> 
> > *Simplify the surd*
> 
> $x==\frac{2\pm\sqrt{4\times13}}{6}=\frac{2\pm2\sqrt{13}}{6}$
> 
> > *Simplify the fraction*
> 
> $x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{13}}{3}$
> 
> $x=\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}{3}\mathrm{or}x=\frac{1-\sqrt{13}}{3}$

title: 2D Coordinates
bodyMd:
# 2D Coordinates

## 2D Coordinates

> **Spec point** — `3.3B`

## 2D coordinates

### What is the Cartesian plane?

- The **Cartesian plane** is a **two-dimensional **grid that has

  - a** horizontal** scale, called the** *****x*****-axis**
  - a** vertical **scale, called the** *****y*****-axis**
- The two** **axes** meet** at the **origin**

  - where ***x  *****and***** y  *****are both 0**

### What are coordinates?

- **Coordinates** are a** pair **of **numbers**, *x * and *y *, that describe the** location** of a **point **on the grid

  - They are written in **brackets** as **(*****x *****, *****y *****)**
  - The point is
  
    - ***x ***** units **on the **horizontal** scale
    - ***y*****  units **on the **vertical **scale
- The **origin** is **(0, 0)**

  - **Positive** values of ***x **** *are to the **right** of the origin
  
    - **Negative** values are to the **left**
  - **Positive** values of ***y***  are **above** the origin
  
    - **Negative** values are **below**
- For example, from the origin:

  - (2, 5) is the point 2 units to the **right** and 5 units **up**
  - (-1, -4) is the point 1 unit to the** left **and 4 units **down**
- "Along the corridor, up the stairs" helps to remember** horizontal **then **vertical**,* ***(*****x *****, *****y*****)**

> **Exam Hint**
> Check the scale on the coordinate grid! 1 square might not represent 1 unit.

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Write down the coordinates of the point *A *shown on the axes below.
> 
> ![2d-coordinates-we](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/aa2a3a825385-42010-coordinates-we.png)
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *A** is 3 units to left, so **x ** is −3*
> *A** is 4 units up, so **y  **is 4*
> *Give your answer in brackets*
> 
> **Final answer:** **(−3, 4)**
> 
> (b) Mark the point *B*  with coordinates (3,- 2) on the same set of axes.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Start at the origin*
> *Count 3 units right and two units down*
> *Mark the point with a solid circle or cross and label it **B*
> 
> ![6j_PGh2e_2d-coordinates-we-answer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/839c3d813eb8-39581-2d-coordinates-we-answer.png)

title: Gradient of a Line
bodyMd:
# Gradient of a Line

## Gradient of a Line

> **Spec point** — `3.3G`

## Gradient of a line

### What is the gradient of a line?

- The** gradient **is a measure of how **steep** a straight line is
- A gradient of 3 means:

  - For every **1 unit** to the right, go **up** by 3
- A gradient of -4 means:

  - For every **1 unit **to the right, go **down** by 4
- A gradient of 3 is **steeper** than 2

  - A gradient of -5 is **steeper **than -4
- A **positive** gradient means the line goes **upwards** (uphill)

  - Bottom left to top right
- A** negative** gradient means the line goes **downwards** (downhill)
- Top left to bottom right

### How do I find the gradient of a line?

- Find** two points** on the line and draw a** right-angled triangle**

  - Then $\mathrm{gradient}=\frac{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in}y}{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in}x}$
  - Or, in short, $\frac{\mathrm{rise}}{\mathrm{run}}$
  
    - The **rise** is the vertical length of the triangle
    - The **run** is the horizontal length of the triangle
  - Put the correct **sign** on your answer
  
    - **Positive **for uphill lines
    - **Negative** for downhill lines
  - You can also find gradient of a line between two points, $\left(x_{1} ,  y_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{2} ,  y_{2}\right)$
  
    - Use the formula  $\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-x_{1}}$

### How do I draw a line with a given gradient?

- To draw the gradient $\frac{2}{3}$

  - The **rise** is 2
  - The **run** is 3
  - It is **positive** (uphill)
  
    - Move 3 units to the **right** and 2 units **up**
- To draw the gradient $-5$ make it a fraction, $-\frac{5}{1}$

  - The **rise** is 5
  - The **run** is 1
  - It is **negative** (downhill)
  
    - Move 1 unit to the **right** and 5 units **down**

> **Exam Hint**
> A lot of students forget to make their gradients negative for downhill lines!

> **Worked Example**
> (a) Find the gradient of the line shown in the diagram below.
> 
> ![screenshot-2023-02-12-at-20-42-17](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/1e70e36014ef-11069-gradient-of-a-line-1.png)
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Find two points that the line passes through*
> 
> $\left(0 ,  2\right)  and  \left(1 ,  5\right)$
> 
> > *Use the grid to draw a right-angled triangle*
> *Find the 'rise' (vertical length) and 'run' (horizontal length)*
> 
> ![cie-igcse-core-gradient-of-a-line-rn-we-a](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/a99db6ef57e1-33454-gradient-of-a-line-2.png)
> 
> > *Work out the fraction *$\frac{\mathrm{rise}}{\mathrm{run}}$
> 
> $\frac{3}{1}=3$
> 
> > *Look to see if the line is uphill or downhill*
> 
> *uphill, so the gradient is positive*
> 
> **Final answer:** **The gradient is 3**
> 
> (b) On the grid below, draw the line with a gradient of −2 that passes through (0,1).

> **Answer:**
> 
> > *Mark on the point (0, 1)*
> *-2 is the fraction *$-\frac{2}{1}$
> *The rise is 2, the run is 1, the line goes downhill (so 1 across, 2 down)*
> 
> ![cie-igcse-gradients-of-lines-we-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-RevisionNotes/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-1/assets/8e4325db44b4-31161-igcse-gradients-of-lines-we-1.png)
